maintopic: CRASH NEAR BRAMPTON IN 1954   REPORT OF TECHNICAL BOARD OF INQUIRY

speakeroldname: Hon. George C. Marler (Minister of Transport):
maintopic: CRASH NEAR BRAMPTON IN 1954   REPORT OF TECHNICAL BOARD OF INQUIRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I table herewith, in
English and French, the report of the technical board of inquiry which I established to investigate the accident to a T.C.A. Lockheed aircraft near Brampton, Ontario, on December 17, 1954. The document tabled, contains the report of the board, the appendices, transcript of evidence, and certain of the principal exhibits.
Having regard to the exhaustive inquiry made by the board and the positive nature of its findings, I have come to the conclusion that no useful purpose would be served by setting up a public board of inquiry as I originally contemplated.
It will be noted that in its report the board made certain suggestions concerning equipment for air traffic control. These sug gestions are receiving careful consideration by my department and so far as it is feasible to do so they will be implemented. The board has also made certain recommendations as to the relationship between airline captains and airline first officers; these recommendations are being taken up by my department with the major Canadian air lines.

On the orders of the day:
Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime
Minister): Mr. Speaker, may I refer to the question asked on Monday, February 14, by the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) regarding the contribution by Canada to the distant early warning screen. As I have made clear, the provision of this distant early warning system is a jointly conceived Canada-United States project. The
1376	HOUSE OF
Inquiries of the Ministry joint plan calls for two early warning lines, one north of the settled areas of Canada and known generally as the mid-Canada line, and a second line across the most northerly practicable part of North America, known generally as the distant early warning line.
These two lines will supplement the presently operating control and warning line known as the "Pinetree" line.
Canada has undertaken to finance, construct and operate the mid-Canada line, and the United States has undertaken responsibility for the construction of the distant early warning line.
In addition to undertaking the mid-Canada line, Canada will, in respect of the distant early warning line, contribute such resources of the R.C.A.F. and the R.C.N. as can be made available, and will assist the United States in organizing and using other Canadian resources.
The participation of Canada in the operation of that line is still under consideration, and we will not be in a position to make any decision about that until more is known about the numbers and the technical skills required in connection with that distant line.
The outline I have given is a short paraphrase of two joint Canada-United States announcements made on September 27 and November 19, 1954, which were published at the time; but it might be the wish of the house to have them on record, and if so, I should be glad to table them at this time.

May I ask the Prime Minister a couple of questions arising out of his statement? What would be the total cost of the three radar protective screens? What proportion of that total cost will Canada bear in relation to the United States contribution? In order to remove the idea that some people have, that the joint venture of the United States and Canada may in some way be an invasion of or an impingement on Canada's sovereignty, what are the terms of the agreement with the United States to assure that there shall not be any invasion of that sovereignty?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
With respect to the first question, it is not possible at this time to state what proportion Canada will be bearing in the joint enterprise that consists of the three warning lines. I can say that, with respect to the "Pinetree" line, it is approximately one-third. The mid-Canada line is being taken care of in its entirety, both as to cost of construction and the commitment of operation by Canada. The other line is one about which no estimates that one could hope would be anything more than a guess could be made. The hon. gentleman knows


what the conditions are in the northernmost points at which the line can be established. It is a matter, with respect to costs, about which nothing accurate can be determined at the present time. Moreover, it has been discussed between the chiefs of staff of United States and our chiefs of staff on the basis that for security reasons it would not be desirable to disclose any figures at this time. Of course, the location of some of these posts will become known because there are some who travel in those remote parts and there will be physical evidence of what is being done. But it was agreed that there would be no statements made either in Washington or here without prior notice to each other.
With respect to the invasion of Canadian sovereignty, nothing has been done that does not flow quite naturally and appropriately from the commitments we have made under the North Atlantic treaty for the common defence of the area envisaged in that treaty. These three lines have been regarded as something essential as a part of the build-up of the joint defence, and the allocation of responsibility for certain services has been made under the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, and every other member of the organization is pledged to assist whatever member of the organization is charged with certain responsibilities.
With respect to the "Pinetree" line, for example, we did not have, and we have not yet, sufficient qualified personnel to operate the whole of it; but it has been stipulated that progressively, as we do find it possible to replace the United States personnel in those radar stations, it will be our privilege to do so. That is the general policy that underlines, according to a declaration that was made quite a long time ago, that anything done on the territory of the other country by Canada or the United States would remain under the control of the authorities of the country where the operation was being carried out. It is no longer possible to be isolated from each other. This is something which is regarded as necessary for the protection of the North American continent and requires to be done as far from vulnerable points as possible, and on the North American continent, from the north, the farthest points are Canadian territory.

subtopic: REPORTED OBJECTION TO USE OF WORD "ROYAL" IN NAME OF TRANSCONTINENTAL TRAIN

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: REPORTED OBJECTION TO USE OF WORD "ROYAL" IN NAME OF TRANSCONTINENTAL TRAIN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Prime Minister. Has the
Prime Minister any comments to make to the house in regard to the positive statement in Sunday's edition of the New York Times that the Canadian Pacific Railway planned to call its new transcontinental train the "Royal Canadian", but that the government objected to this and as a result part of the name, "Royal", has been dropped?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: REPORTED OBJECTION TO USE OF WORD "ROYAL" IN NAME OF TRANSCONTINENTAL TRAIN
speechtext:
No, Mr. Speaker, I was quite surprised to hear anything about that. When my attention was called to a newspaper report this morning, I had not heard of it at all.
I have had inquiries made to find out what, if any, are the facts which would justify that kind of an assertion. I have seen the suggestion that it was because this government disliked the word "royal". Well, that is nonsense. The constitution of this country is a monarchial constitution and I have always asserted, and I know that is-well, I hope it is-the unanimous sentiment of every hon. member in this house, that that is the best kind of constitution for the Canadian people that we could hope for.
Any suggestion that there is any dislike of that kind of constitution or of the proper use of the word "royal" is quite beside the point. I have declared many times that wherever it is proper the word "royal" should be used. It is unhesitatingly used when the consent of Her Majesty has been obtained. Of course, that is a part of the monarch's prerogative and we never attempt to use the word "royal" in any descriptive title without prior approval by the monarch. All hon. members know what are the many places in which it is used, namely, the Royal Canadian Navy, the Royal Canadian Air Force, the Royal Canadian Artillery or Regiment, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, the Royal Mail, and many others.
Under our constitution the executive government of this country is vested in Her Majesty. We all remember what was the unanimous feeling of this house a couple of years ago when a bill was introduced having to do with the royal style and titles as proper for use in Canada. We were all unanimous that Her Majesty should be described as the Queen of the United Kingdom and Canada, and we all asserted that it was as Queen of the United Kingdom that we were proud to have Her Majesty as the Queen of Canada because that recalled the historical development of our Canadian institutions. Her Majesty is the beloved Queen of Canada because she is Queen of the United Kingdom and because historically the monarch of the United Kingdom has been monarch of this land as well as of the United Kingdom from at least 1763. Any suggestion
1378	HOUSE OF
Inquiries of the Ministry that there is any republican feeling is a suggestion that is quite foreign to me and I hope quite foreign to all hon. members of this house.

subtopic: REPORTED OBJECTION TO USE OF WORD "ROYAL" IN NAME OF TRANSCONTINENTAL TRAIN
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am sure that hon. members throughout the house will agree with the sentiments expressed by the Prime Minister, but my remarks were directed to a positive statement appearing in a very reliable publication. I would suggest that it might be desirable that a statement be made as soon as appropriately possible dealing with this particular case which has been described in such positive terms.

May
I ask the Prime Minister a supplementary question? I am in agreement with what the Prime Minister has said, but should not the use of the word "royal" be confined to institutions and organizations intimately connected with the government of Canada. The government might find itself bombarded with requests to use the word "royal" in connection with this, that and everything. Should it not be confined to governmental institutions or organizations?

subtopic: REPORTED OBJECTION TO USE OF WORD "ROYAL" IN NAME OF TRANSCONTINENTAL TRAIN
speechtext: I think it is usually confined to governmental institutions, but there are exceptions. The most recent one that I remember is when the permission of Her Majesty was obtained to call the Winnipeg ballet the Royal Winnipeg Ballet.

Mr. Speaker, I have two questions for the Secretary of State for External Affairs having to do with the Pacific area. The first is this. Has Canada an observer at the southeast Asia defence treaty conference in Bangkok? If not, have any arrangements been made so the Canadian government will be kept informed of the proceedings?
My second question is this. Can the minister give the house any information concerning the report by the prime minister of Thailand that his country is threatened by invasion from communist China through a strip of Laos which lies between the two countries and which apparently is communist-dominated?

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in answer to the first question may I say that we have no observer at the conference which opens today jn Bangkok but arrangements have been


made which should ensure that we are adequately informed of what is going on at that conference.
In answer to the second question I may say that we do know that the government of Thailand has been concerned about a possible threat to its security from the adjoining territory of communist China for many months. The possibility of United Nations consideration of this matter has been discussed from time to time. Moreover, the Manila treaty provides for mutual consultation concerning threats to the security of any of the signatories, and so this question may well come before the conference which opens in Bangkok either today or tomorrow.
We have ourselves no specific information which would confirm the existence of the forces mentioned by the prime minister of Thailand in the statement which is attributed to him, but we are aware that the situation in this general area has been unsettled for some time.

May I ask a supplementary
question? Does Canada not have a member on what is known as the international supervisory commission for Laos and, if so, would it not be possible to obtain from him information with regard to this condition?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The international commission for Laos does include a Canadian member as well as Indian and Polish members. Mobile teams from that commission, I understand, have investigated the situation in the northern part of Laos to which my hon. friend has referred.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Prime Minister. Do the remarks attributed to A. D. P. Heeney, Canadian ambassador to
1380	HOUSE OF
Inquiries of the Ministry the United States, made yesterday at Palm Beach, Florida, and reported by the Canadian Press in today's Globe and Mail, reflect the government's official attitude with respect to the organizational arrangements of the British commonwealth of nations?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO PRESS REPORT OF REMARKS BY A. D. P. HEENEY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not sure what the ambassador said about the organizational arrangements. The hon. gentleman sent me a clipping in which Mr. Heeney is reported to have-
. . . described the British commonwealth as an "example to the world of how nations can survive and prosper in mutual friendship and respect."
I think that view is fairly widely shared by his fellow Canadians. The report goes on to say-not as a quotation but as a summary, I suppose, of what the ambassador said-as follows:
The commonwealth, he said, is a co-operative and voluntary association of sovereign states committed in their dealings with one another to the principles of peace and justice.
I think we are all committed to one another in the pursuit of peace and justice. Whether the word "co-operative" has just the right connotation or not, I do not know. I know it is an association where we are happy to co-operate with one another and where we each do our best to serve our interests in serving the interests of the other members of the commonwealth. According to the report he adds this comment:
It straddled the continents and cut across racial divisions and cultures.
I think that is also something which is fairly generally admitted. I think we all appreciate the fact that it is perhaps the most effective bridge we now have between the East and the. West.

subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO PRESS REPORT OF REMARKS BY A. D. P. HEENEY
speechtext: Perhaps the Prime Minister would permit a supplementary question. A little further on in the clipping which I sent to the Prime Minister, the import of Mr. Heeney's remarks seems to be that the British commonwealth is an easy-going discussion group. That seemed to be the import of them. Would the Prime Minister care to comment on that matter?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO PRESS REPORT OF REMARKS BY A. D. P. HEENEY
speechtext:
I can assure the hon. gentleman that when we meet the discussions are always easy-going. I notice that a part of the quotation indicates that in the discussions between the ambassadors in Washington and other capitals, it is possible:
... "to discuss with special frankness and candour our differences as well as our agreements." Such consultations went on in and between the various capitals around the world.
Although such consultations rarely result in anything approaching common policies, there can be


no doubt that the effect of this friendly confrontation of differing interests and viewpoints helps us all to avoid extremes and to make full allowance for the attitudes of our friends.
Is that the part the hon. gentleman had in mind?

subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO PRESS REPORT OF REMARKS BY A. D. P. HEENEY
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO PRESS REPORT OF REMARKS BY A. D. P. HEENEY
speechtext: That is also quite true but I think it is a far from complete statement of the value to us all of commonwealth relationships.

I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Agriculture. Is the minister aware of the fact that Macedonian toad flax is being advertised for sale as a flower? In view of the persistence of toad flax as a noxious weed in many areas of Canada, what steps does the minister propose to take to stop it?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Gardiner (Minister of Agriculture):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Kindersley was kind enough to send me a copy of his question. In reply I wish to state that the control of weeds is a provincial and municipal responsibility.
I am advised by the botany division of the central experimental farm that they have never collected a specimen of Macedonian toad flax in Saskatchewan that they are sure of. They do not know if Macedonian is definitely a weed threat. There is no legislation that forbids a seed house selling a plant such as Macedonian toad flax. It is an ornamental flower.
Common toad flax is the danger in Saskatchewan. It is native to Canada. Funds are made available by the federal Department of Agriculture to the University of Saskatchewan in connection with its control. Our officials are very much aware of the common toad flax problem. There is no federal legislation to control unless it gets into commercial seed. They do not know if Macedonian is definitely a weed threat.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. Yesterday the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marler), on behalf of the Canadian National Railways, dealt with certain questions-a set in my name and a set in the name of the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker)-regarding lay-offs on the Canadian National Railways. The house will recall that our questions were not answered in the way we felt they should be answered.
My question of privilege is this. Last year a similar question was answered on three different occasions. On January 22, 1954, as recorded at page 1356 of Hansard, the parliamentary assistant to the then minister of transport indicated that at that time 800 employees had been laid off by the Canadian National Railways. On February 11, 1954, as recorded at page 1983 of Hansard, the then minister of transport indicated that the number had risen to 1,500. On May 20, 1954, as recorded at pages 4901 and 4902 of Hansard,
Inquiries of the Ministry the then minister of transport indicated that another 600, in addition to the 1,500, had been laid off. I hope that the present Minister of Transport will take note of this question of privilege and will see if he cannot get from the Canadian National Railways an answer supplementary to the figures that were given to us last year. In other words, can he not get from the Canadian National Railways up-to-date information, corresponding to the figures we were given last year, as to the numbers that have now been laid off?

subtopic: LAY-OFFS    REFERENCE TO ANSWERS GIVEN BY MINISTER

Arising out of the question of privilege of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), I want to refer particularly to one portion of the reply given yesterday by the Minister of Transport to the question I asked to which the hon. member made reference. My question was:
How many section and maintenance men of the Canadian National Railways have been laid off by (a) regions; (b) divisions, since the first day of January, 1955?
This question was answered in part as follows:
This is another question which cannot be answered completely without the assignment of a special staff.
I should like to ask the minister this question. Does Canadian National Railways not keep a record as to the number of section and maintenance men laid off which would obviate the necessity of this large or special staff in order to compile the total?

subtopic: LAY-OFFS    REFERENCE TO ANSWERS GIVEN BY MINISTER

subtopic: REPORTED CONSIDERATION OF SALE OF NORTHWEST SYSTEMS

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. George C. Marler (Minister of Transport):
subtopic: REPORTED CONSIDERATION OF SALE OF NORTHWEST SYSTEMS
speechtext:
I should like to reply to a
question of last Friday when the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) asked if the sale or other disposition of the northwest communications system or the Alberta-Saskatchewan section of the government telegraph and telephone service or either of them was under active consideration. The answer to the hon. member's question is no. If a specific proposal should be received it would, of course, be given consideration.

The house resumed, from Friday, February 18, consideration of the motion of Mr. Harris for committee of supply.

Mr. Speaker, I desire to rise on this motion for the purpose of expressing a grievance. Before so doing, may I point out that the fact that I am raising a new grievance will automatically put an end to any further debate on the subject that was previously under discussion. I take it that I may go ahead with this matter unless somebody else has something further to say on the grievance previously under debate.
Go ahead.

As nobody else rises, I presume I can proceed with my grievance. I have a very definite grievance which I feel should be brought forward on this motion. Generally speaking, the grievance is the lack of information as to government policy regarding the endeavours of the government in the export trade field. I raise the matter particularly because of the answer I was given by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) to a question I asked on February 18, which is to be found at page 1281 of Hansard. On that day I asked the minister the following question:
I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. Has the government

turned down an application for an export permit by the East-West Export-Import Company, Vancouver, requesting permission to export Canadian built cargo ships to the U.S.S.R.? If so, will the minister explain to the house the reason for that, and will the department reconsider the application?
1 received the following reply to that question from the Minister of Trade and Commerce:
The department has not in actual fact turned down an application, Mr. Speaker, for the export of a ship, since the ship does not exist. The department was consulted as to whether Canada would be prepared to export ships of certain types to the U.S.S.R. We were able to say that certain types would be authorized and certain types would not be authorized. We pointed out which types were which. We are quite sure there was no bona fide requirement behind the application. In other words, we are quite sure that no order had been placed by the U.S.S.R. or was about to be placed in this particular case.
I raise this grievance, Mr. Speaker, because I am convinced that the attitude of the government on matters of this nature is completely wrong and detrimental to the commonwealth of Canada. May I say, sir, that in speaking on another occasion I said "commonwealth of Canada" and in Hansard my words were changed to "Dominion of Canada." It is my understanding that we are now the commonwealth of Canada.
We certainly are not.

Canada is an export nation. We live and thrive because we are an export nation. Over a matter of months there have been editorials in newspapers throughout the length and breadth of the dominion, the implication of which has been that Canada in its export policies is either tied up to or is giving way to the influence of the United States. It is not my intention to engage in any diatribe against the United States with respect to our relations with that country, but I do feel that we have reached a time when, in view of our economic situation in Canada, our unemployment, and all the briefs that are being received by members of parliament, there should be complete clarification of what is the export and import policy of Canada.
There should be a complete understanding, and it has not yet been made clear either by the government generally or by the Minister of Trade and Commerce in particular whether our policy is unduly influenced by the United States or whether, being a partner in the British commonwealth, we are influenced by and support other members of the commonwealth and those democratic countries outside the commonwealth. It is my privilege, sir, to be now attending my second session of this House of Commons. I feel it is time we faced up to the attitude of government which

should very definitely be considered a grievance, and that is that because we are fearful of certain countries in the matter of war, although we are not at war, we view with suspicion every proposal which is made. I am speaking now specifically on the matter of exports and imports.
I want to deal specifically with our shipyards, although I know it is possible to deal also with other phases of this question. Canada is a nation which, because of harbours and established industries, is blessed with opportunities for building ships of many and varying types. I want to wait, Mr. Speaker, for one moment. I have a very powerful voice, but I am not able to hear even my voice because of the conversations taking place in this chamber.
Canada could and should be a shipbuilding nation. During the last war it was conclusively proven what could be done in the way of building ships in both the eastern provinces and on the Pacific coast. Today our yards both east and west are not operating anywhere near full capacity. This means a great loss to our country both from the employer point of view and also from the employee point of view. There have been a number of editorials in the press as to whether or not Canada should use its shipyards for the production of ships of a varying nature for the U.S.S.R. There has also been a brief submitted to the members of the House of Commons. I am told that under date of February 9 of this year the Vancouver daily Sun stated this:
A hot international issue has developed over Russian overtures to build cargo ships in Canada, a proposition in which a British Columbia shipyard has shown interest.
Ottawa sources said today Russian attempts to have the ships built in this country have raised the ire of U.S. government authorities. The U.S. says cargo ships are "strategic" and should not be sold to Russia.
This brief which I have in my hand, and which I would be glad to table if you so desire, goes on to say:
Britain, Denmark and France are leading a fight-
May I repeat that, sir.
Britain, Denmark and France are leading a fight to have the freighters taken off the strategic material list. Because of this disagreement, a committee representing 17 western block nations, is deadlocked in Paris on discussions concerning trade with iron curtain nations.
The British, Swedish, French, Danish and Dutch are all building or have built ships for Russia, from tankers to cargo vessels, deep sea tugs, trawlers and refrigerated fish carriers.
Now, sir, I think that is a very important statement appearing in a very important newspaper in the Dominion of Canada. As a matter of fact, its circulation is the second
Export Trade
highest in the entire country. To the best of my knowledge, sir, it has never been made clear in Canada as to what are the specifications upon which this government insists in the production of ships of varying types, or whether those specifications are tied in with the policy of the United States or tied in with the policy of Great Britain which, I understand, is similar to that of the democratic countries of France, Denmark, Sweden, and Holland.
I cannot for the life of me understand why the shipyards in Canada should be lying idle, and thousands of shipyard workers be unemployed when in the other democratic countries they do not consider that by building cargo vessels they are supplying strategic material to a country or countries with which the democracies feel they may at some time have to go to war. The question of exports is a paramount one in Canada. The utilization of our industry and the employment of our people is a paramount consideration in Canada. I feel that this government, upon more than one occasion, in its attitude and in the answers given to questions, has been laying a foundation of enmity and not friendship. Not one of us wants war. Not one of us will be derelict in either trying to prevent or being prepared for war. But, sir, when a major country such as the U.S.S.R. makes a request through an intermediary, what kind of answer does this government give? They say, we do not think the offer was made in all sincerity. The exact words were, "It is not a bona fide request".
The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), who made that statement here the other day, is known throughout Canada as an engineer. He is known throughout Canada as a businessman. I was amazed at his answer because he said it was not a question of the sale of a ship because the ship had not been built. Of course it had not, because before any company could proceed to build that ship they had to know whether or not they could obtain an export permit for it. Surely, that is a strictly businesslike approach. The answer was "no", on the ground that this government did not consider it a bona fide approach. They base it, I presume, on the fact that it is considered our shipyards in eastern Canada and in British Columbia could not compete with the prices offered by Great Britain, Denmark, Sweden, France and Holland. But, sir, if a country with which we are not at war desires to open up trade negotiations and do business with Canada, even though it might cost them some money, who are we in Canada to say that we question why they are prepared to do so?

Export Trade
I have read thoroughly and often the brief sent to members of the House of Commons by the East-West Export-Import Company Limited of Vancouver. This is a company that has been in business for almost 20 years in that city, a company that took what I suggest is a businesslike approach, because it was announced through the medium of the press, referring to the Vancouver Sun of October 22, 1954-
Canada is prepared to approve the export of Canadian ships to Russia and her satellites within certain limitations, a high government source said today. Russia, through her embassy here, has made inquiries about the placing of contracts in Canadian shipyards. Earlier this year Soviet ambassador Dmitri Chuvahin said Russia is prepared to buy ships from Canada such as trawlers and freighters.
On the basis of this report the East-West Export-Import Company Limited made inquiries and received a reply, which said:
With reference to your above offer for construction of vessels for us please be informed that we would be ready to consider your offer for cargo motorships of about 10,000 tons deadweight and service speed 17-18 knots subject to prices not being higher than those of your competitors and your assuredness that export licences can be granted.
On the basis of that inquiry, made in all sincerity and honesty, and subject to the granting of export licences by the government of Canada, this legitimate business firm in British Columbia made inquiries as to cost. From whom did they make the inquiries? They were made from the Burrard Dry Dock Company Limited, Canadian Vickers Limited, Victoria Machinery Depot Company Limited and Davie Shipbuilding Limited. As a result of these inquiries they submitted their costs.
It has been said by the Minister of Trade and Commerce: I think it is propaganda and not bona fide. We are living in a world which, at the present time at least, is at peace. We should be a shipbuilding nation. We have our shipyards, with thousands of trained men and women in the shipbuilding industry who are idle. But for reasons not explained by the government it has taken an attitude which I say, sir, helps to foster enmity and not friendship. It would seem that, on the basis of trade, we are afraid of those whom we might fear from a military standpoint.
Sir, irrespective of your fears of the future, you can only build friendship on the ground that "We will meet you at least half way." From all the reports I have, it is possible that we could not meet other nations on a competitive basis in the building of certain types of ships; but if we are not dealing in strategic materials, then, in the interests of our own industry, the employment of our own people and the maintenance of their

skills, why are we not prepared at least to go as far as other democratic countries who believe in democracy as much as we do? Why do we not go as far as they have gone, on a trade relationship basis?
In the 18 months I have been a member of the House of Commons I have failed completely to understand why we should follow the United States so slavishly, instead of honestly and sincerely accepting guidance from Great Britain. That applies not only in the matter of trade but also in external affairs.
As has been said by government representatives in the House of Commons, and Canadian representatives at international conferences, as well as in the press, Canada is in a better position than any other country in the world to give a lead to the world, and could be the leader of a combination of smaller nations outside the three great powers.
I believe I have placed before the house a proper grievance. I, too, look with fear to the future, from a military standpoint. But I may also say that Canada, because of her blunt statement that she questions the honesty and sincerity of a prospective trading nation, is playing power politics of another country, and is not following the lead of Great Britain. Thereby we are rendering a disservice in the interests of internationalism and the maintenance of continued peace.
I believe it is time we heard a full explanation of government policy on trade, an explanation as to why, in a time of peace, we will not follow through to find out whether an offer of trade is honestly made and bona fide, instead of challenging it immediately and saying that it is a lie, that it is propaganda and is not bona fide.
No one in this house has greater antagonism than I have to communism; no one can claim greater antagonism to the policies of the U.S.S.R. But we are interested in peace; and if we have an application for trade, let us deal with it. Let us not say immediately that it is a lie, that it is propaganda. While we may have reservations, let us accept the approaches made, let us study them and follow them through. Secondly, let us not antagonize where this is unnecessary, because, as I said before, Canada is a trading nation. Our economy falls, our standard of living falls, and in particular our shipyards and workers lie idle unless we can obtain more contracts outside of our own requirements in this, our country of Canada.
I have been told that I would be putting my neck out in raising this matter. Well, sir, that is not new to me at all. To me this matter of approach, this matter of considering trade and commerce, is of the utmost

importance to our country and our people.
I feel that Canadians have been kept in the dark as to the actual policy of the government; that Canadians have been misdirected because of statements to the effect that we challenge, that we are afraid of, any offers that are made to us by certain other countries in times of peace. I would not ask, sir, that Canada have any different specifications on the construction of ships of any nature from that of Great Britain or from that of any other democratic country. But we should know whether there is any difference; we should know whether Canada will go along with Great Britain. If so, then our Canadian shipyards should have the same right to deal with any other country as have the countries that I have already named. To me, sir, this is important from the point of view of industry, from the point of view of employment, and from the point of view of trying to build up friendship and not enmity. I sincerely hope that before this motion is passed we shall have a clear exposition from the Minister of Trade and Commerce or from anyone who speaks in his name.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: Mr. Speaker,-
I want to introduce a new grievance if no one else wishes to speak on this matter.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I take it that the senior hon. member for Halifax will deal with the subject matter raised by the hon. member for Vancouver East.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker. If no one else wishes to speak on the grievance that has been raised by the hon. member who has just taken his seat, I should like to accept his invitation, not perhaps to give him a lengthy explanation but to deal with the points that he has raised.
In point of fact, Mr. Speaker, I think I can answer what he has said, and particularly the last few phrases which seem to sum up his concern. All he asked was that Canada should not be guided by specifications other than those recognized by the United Kingdom in connection with matters of this kind. I can assure the hon. member that that is so. The situation in Canada and our international commitments in this connection are exactly the same as those of the United Kingdom. The decisions which are reached in connection with these matters are joint decisions which are participated in by Canada and the United Kingdom equally.
At the beginning and toward the end of his speech the hon. member seemed to be directing his remarks to matters of general trade and general trade policy and the efforts
Export Trade
of Canada to sell in world markets the products of Canadian industry and of Canadian agriculture. But the specific matter with which he dealt at some length was of course obviously in a very restricted field, namely, in the field of trade with countries behind the iron curtain in items which come within the category of strategic items which could possibly be put to other than civilian or commercial use.
The hon. member complained that the house had been kept in the dark in connection with government policy in this regard.
I should remind him and the house, Mr. Speaker, that in the last session of parliament the Export and Import Permits Act was completely reviewed by this house. The act was re-enacted with a number of amendments, and there was quite a full debate on the various readings of that bill and in the committee of the whole house. If the hon. member wishes, he can discover government policy in connection with these matters by simply looking up the debates in Hansard of last session. If he does that, I think he will see that most of the questions he has posed this afternoon were answered in the course of the various stages of that debate. However, he has raised a specific point with which I think I should deal.
First of all, I will summarize briefly the situation in so far as Canada is concerned. With a view to co-ordinating export controls of strategic materials from this country and from other similar-minded countries, 15 of the democratic countries of the free world, which include Canada, the United States, the United Kingdom, most of our NATO partners and Japan, have established under the auspices of NATO a committee called the international co-ordinating committee, on which we have permanent representation, together with the other countries participating. This committee considers the type of materials and products which can, with safety, be traded in with countries behind the iron curtain. This committee, by unanimous decision, has listed certain arms, munitions, implements of war and strategic materials which those countries, each one individually, have agreed to withhold from the Soviet bloc countries. The United Kingdom is a partner to that agreement to withhold to exactly the same extent as Canada is. Along with arms, munitions and implements of war, certain ships have been regarded, and have been listed by that committee, as of strategic importance. Whether a ship is strategic in this sense or not depends on its specifications, its speed and the details of construction and equipment. All of those 15 countries

Export Trade
govern themselves by exactly the same regulations and considerations in deciding on the strategic or non-strategic nature of ships.
May I ask a question?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: Yes.

Is the representative of Canada on that committee backing up the request of Great Britain that the limitation on specifications be put aside to bring in cargo vessels? What stand is Canada taking on that matter?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: From time to time discussions take place in this committee with respect to changes in various regulations relating to a variety of items. It is obvious that the changing situation in the world would require that kind of discussion. I am not in position to advise the hon. member of the specific position taken by the United Kingdom or the United States or even by ourselves in those discussions.
By Canada.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: All I can add is that the decisions which were taken by the committee were on a basis of unanimity and that the actual regulations which are observed by Canada are those which have been accepted by the United Kingdom just as they have been accepted by us.
Will the hon. member explain why he is not in a position to tell us what position Canada is taking on the matter?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
speechtext:
I am telling the hon. member that we are not in a position, and I am not in a position, because I simply have not that information, to disclose to the hon. member what the attitude of Great Britain is on any specific question of this kind, or whether or not in discussing matters of this kind we have taken positions that are or are not in support of any views that the Great Britain representative might disclose or not. All I am saying to the hon. member is that these decisions have been taken unanimously by the committee and that Great Britain is committed to exactly the same regulations as we are.
I submit that that disposes of the main point that the hon. member made just at the end when he was insisting that we be governed by the same specifications, with respect to the strategic nature of ships, as is the United Kingdom. That is exactly the position at the present time, and so long as this committee operates on its present basis that will continue to be the position.
With reference to the particular matter of the approaches made to the Department of Trade and Commerce by the East-West Export-Import Company of Vancouver for
TMr. Dickey.]
an export permit for a ship of 15,000 tons, what they indicated was a 10,000 ton cargo vessel of 17 to 18 knots speed. I think it was indicated to be a general cargo motor ship of 15,500 tons displacement with a speed of 17 to 18 knots.
I understood the hon. member to say that he was informed that East-West Export-Import Company Limited had been organized and operating for some 20 years. The information that we have is that this company was incorporated only in September 1954. So far as we can determine, it is a new company without any background of dealings either in shipping matters or in trading matters of other kinds.
The answer which the department gave to that company was as follows:
With respect to your inquiry regarding the control of exports of ships to Russia and satellite countries, generally speaking, export permits would not be granted covering merchant ships, particularly of the size indicated in the proposal which you recently submitted to this department. Similarly, permits would not be granted for naval vessels or vessels with special characteristics or possibilities which would permit their conversion to naval uses. We would consider the specifications of the tugs or fishing vessels on their individual merits. Perhaps you would be good enough to inform us if your clients are prepared to place firm orders with you on the basis of detailed specifications.
According to the advice I have received up to today no firm order or detailed specifications have been forthcoming regarding the proposed applicant. The hon. member did not indicate that he had any information which would disclose that any shipyard or any other company of that kind had received any order or firm inquiry for ships of this nature, either directly from Russian sources or from the proposed applicant, the East-West Export-Import Company Limited.

I quoted from the information sent to a number of members of parliament that after receipt of information from the agency in the U.S.S.R. they had made inquiries of certain companies as to the cost of these ships.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
speechtext:
In that connection I noticed the quotation which the hon. member gave from this brief prepared by the East-West Export-Import Company Limited, and I quote from the second page:
Immediately upon receipt of this we opened up negotiations with Burrard Dry Dock Co. Ltd., Canadian Vickers Ltd., Victoria Machinery Depot Co. Ltd. and Davie Shipbuilding Ltd. and obtained quotations from these firms for the construction of the type of vessel requested. Subsequently an application was made to the Department of Trade and Commerce for the necessary export permit which has been rejected.
That is exactly what I quoted.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
speechtext:
The fact is that the department has not received from the companies named therein, or from any other shipyard, any proposal or suggestion which could in any sense be considered a firm order or even a reasonable inquiry in connection with the building of such a ship. No responsible member of the Canadian shipbuilding industry has given the slightest support to this application or proposed application for a permit.
I think it is significant and disposes pretty effectively of the hon. member's representation that no member of our shipbuilding industry, which is actively looking for every possibility of employing its facilities, has yet received any inquiry from the Soviet bloc for the classes of vessel for which it is clear that export permits would be issued.
In his speech the hon. member referred to a press conference given some months ago by the Soviet ambassador in connection with Canadian-Soviet trade. At that time the Soviet ambassador is reported to have said that his country would be interested in buying trawlers and cargo ships. The indication has always been definite that export permits for ships such as tugs and trawlers would be granted. However, no inquiry of this nature has been received. The type of inquiries which are directed here, and the inquiry received from the East-West Export-Import Company Limited to which the hon. member referred is of that type, appear to be only for the class of vessel for which approval cannot be obtained, either from Canada or from our partners in the international coordinating committee. On that basis I think I can advise the hon. member and the house that everything connected with this proposed application for a permit indicates that this is not a bona fide application to which we could look for any substantial business, and it is one which would have to be turned down on the facts so far disclosed. But if the East-West Export-Import Company Limited comes forward with a proposal for the kind of vessels that we can export, and if those proposals seem to be regarded as interesting by bona fide shipbuilders in Canada, they certainly will receive every co-operation and encouragement from the department.

subtopic: SALES TO VETERANS IN HAMILTON AND PETERBOROUGH
SALES TO VETERANS IN HAMILTON AND PETERBOROUGH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to direct my grievance to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Winters). I am speaking on behalf of two organized bodies of veterans, one in Hamilton and the other in Peterborough. Those veterans are
Housing-Sales to Veterans at the present time living in houses that were built by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation back in 1949, I think it was, especially for veterans. Recently the government has offered to sell these houses to the veterans who are renting them at the present time.
I have no criticism of that move on the part of the government. As a matter of fact, from the veterans themselves I learn that they are rather anxious to buy those houses. Most of them have lived in those houses for five years. Some of them have spent considerable sums of money in upkeep, repairs and beautifying the houses inside and out, and they have become attached to them. Another reason why they are rather anxious to buy them is that these houses now provide about the only chance these veterans have of securing low-cost houses. These veterans are certainly in no position to make the down payment and the annual payments on houses newly constructed at today's prices. These houses built five years ago, on a mass-production scale, should provide an opportunity whereby these veterans may be able to secure houses at a cost considerably lower than that of new houses. However, the criticism is of the price that the department is asking for those houses.
I am told that the price asked is, generally speaking, $8,700 with the option of a reduction of $1,000 provided the purchaser continues to live in the house for five years, or a proportionate reduction for whatever part of the five years he lives in these houses. The complaint that I have heard is that $8,700 is at least $2,000 more than the houses are worth at the present time, although not necessarily more than the present market value, because almost any kind of a house today can fetch a fairly high market value. By responsible contractors I am told that the houses were built five years ago for not more than $6,700 or $6,800. I am assured that if the government paid more than $6,800 as the top price for those houses five years ago, they paid more than the houses were then worth. If that be so, even after allowing for the $1,000 reduction over five years, the government would still stand to make a profit of $1,000 on each of those houses.
In the first place I want to say-and in this I am sure the minister will agree with me-that 1 do not think this country is in such dire economic straits that it must exploit the natural desire of a veteran to own a house in order to profit at his expense. I am quite sure that the minister is the last person in this country who would want to do that. I am confident that the minister is ill advised if he has been persuaded that these houses are worth $8,700.
1388	HOUSE OF
Housing-Sales to Veterans
I have discussed the matter with Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. They have given me three reasons for asking the present price. First, they say that $8,700 is a fair and reasonable price in the light of today's market value. Of course the question is whether the government, in view of the fact that these veterans have occupied these houses for five years, is going to insist on collecting the full present market value of those houses or whether the government is prepared to give these veterans a bit of a break. I have visited a number of the houses in both of these projects, and I am convinced that the government is asking more than these houses are worth even at today's market value.
The second reason given was that if the government were to sell these houses for less than $8,700 to the veterans who occupy them, they would be playing favourites with this particular group of veterans and that it would be unfair to the veterans who have built their own homes or who have purchased other houses. I doubt that the government would be subject to much criticism if by any chance these veterans should get these houses at a little bit lower cost than the price paid by some other veteran for another type of house. In any case I know that the veterans organization, the Canadian Legion, in Peterborough and in Hamilton support these organized groups and certainly they have given no indication that veterans as a whole would feel that this particular group were getting any special favour by securing these houses at a lower price.
A third reason given to me was that when these houses are sold a substantial part of the selling price must go to the municipality concerned in return for land and service privileges. My understanding is that the rent charged for these houses during the past five years was supposed to take care of the service charges which the government was paying to the municipalities. I have before me the agreement made between the city of Peterborough and Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation setting forth the terms on which these houses are to be sold and just what compensation the municipality is to receive, and for the life of me I cannot see how the municipality can be blamed for the price that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is charging the veterans for those houses.
We have had reputable contractors estimate just what it will cost to bring these particular houses up to or near the standard of the new houses of similar size which are being built and sold under the auspices of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation in those municipalities. I refer particularly now to the group in Hamilton. I have the


details of the group in Peterborough and I will give them later. The Hamilton houses are storey and a half, five-room houses built of asbestos sheathing or siding. They have no eavestroughing and no sidewalks. There are wooden beams in the basements contrary to the Hamilton city building bylaw. They have gyproc walls with no plaster. There are no doors on the clothes closets. There are mutual side drives which are wide enough for one car only. Each sewer is connected to two houses so that if one tenant's sewer is blocked the other fellow is in trouble as well.
According to estimates which the veterans have received it will require $700 to plaster these houses inside. It will cost $200 to instal eavestroughing with drains connected to the sewers. It will cost $40 to put doors on all clothes closets and $50 to build sidewalks. It will take $400 to put in laundry tubs and to tile the kitchens in the way that the new houses are tiled. Houses with all these conveniences are built under Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation auspices in Hamilton and are selling for $10,000. If the houses to which I have referred were restored to the standard of new houses the purchasers would be required to spend $1,450, which would bring the price of these houses well above the present price of new houses. They would then have houses built with asbestos sheathing instead of brick. They would still have old houses that do not in any sense measure up to the standards of the new houses which are selling at $10,000.
The Peterborough people have submitted similar estimates, and these are their complaints about the condition of the houses. There is no plastered wall construction in the Peterborough houses. They are said to be unsatisfactorily insulated. Much of the material used in the construction is of inferior quality. Some of the Peterborough houses have aluminum siding instead of asbestos. The doors are very poorly fitted. The floors give evidence of the fact that uncured lumber was used. The electrical fixtures are of a very inferior standard and are poorly installed. Many of the basements become very wet and leak violently in wet weather. Repairs have had to be made to some of them because of the unsanitary condition arising from seepage into the basements. The roofs of some of the units leak and the interior decorations have suffered accordingly. Most of the maintenance work and improvements that have been carried out on these houses during the past five years have been done by the veterans themselves.
My whole purpose in raising this question is in the hope that the minister will reconsider the price which is being asked for these

houses. I may tell the minister that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation sold a group of houses in Hamilton two years ago that in my opinion, and again I compared both, are superior to those that are now being sold for $6,800. They were sold for 10 per cent down, as is being asked for these, and the interest rate was 4i per cent instead of the 5J per cent that is being charged for these particular groups of houses.
I called this matter to the attention of the officials of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, and they assured me that these veterans' houses are superior to the ones that were sold two years ago for $6,800. I assure the minister that if I wanted to purchase a house in either of these two groups I would prefer one of the houses that were sold two years ago at the same price at which these are being offered to the veterans at the present time. I suggest that in the general interests of the veterans themselves the minister or Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation should discuss the matter with the Department of Veterans Affairs. In my contacts with the Department of Veterans Affairs I have found that they are always willing to show a little milk of human kindness in their dealings with veterans. I have found that in every instance they are willing to give the veteran the benefit of the doubt, if at all possible.

There is no great rush on the part of veterans to buy them. The latest report I have as of January 6 indicates that in Peterborough five houses had been sold and two others had been vacant and up for sale for two months and had not been sold. No, five houses had been vacant and up for sale for two months without being sold. Of the eight that have been sold to date, only four were sold to veteran tenants and the other four were sold to non-tenants. I do not know whether or not they were veterans. Only four of the eight were sold to veteran tenants and the other four were disposed of to nontenants. There is no great rush on the part
Housing-Sales to Veterans of veterans to buy these houses. I should like the minister to reconsider the price placed on these houses, and let us see if we cannot give the veterans a little better break.

subtopic: SALES TO VETERANS IN HAMILTON AND PETERBOROUGH
speechtext:
I should like to say a word in support of what has been said by the hon. member who has just taken his seat. I am not familiar with the situation in either Peterborough or Hamilton, but as the hon. member said a moment ago I do know that the Department of Veterans Affairs has endeavoured to provide houses for veterans as cheaply as possible. During our committee meetings last year, this was one of the subjects that we discussed. It was explained to us then that since 1949, when these men first occupied these houses in Peterborough and Hamilton, the cost of construction had gone up by some 80 per cent, possibly represented by labour cost increases. This would mean that the price of the house when these veterans first rented it would be much less than the present price.
Now, the whole purpose of our program in the veterans committee last year with reference to houses was to give all the assistance possible to veterans in the construction of their own homes. Towards that end, schools were to be set up in which the veteran would be instructed in the general principles of house construction. As I say, every effort was to be made to provide the veterans with cheaper homes. It does seem to me, as has been suggested by the hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy), that assistance could be given to the veterans to purchase these homes just the same as assistance was being given to enable veterans to build their own homes, that is, if we wish veterans to own their own homes, and I am sure we all do.
There is nothing further I wish to say in that connection except this, and I am not sure it has any particular bearing on the subject. I do feel there is too much concentration, not only in veterans endeavouring to build their own homes but other people in general, in the larger centres like Hamilton, Toronto and Montreal. I feel that this problem of veterans homes, as well as the problem of homes for other people, could be very well solved if there were a greater decentralization in this country. It could be solved if we were to build homes not only in Hamilton, Peterborough, Toronto and Montreal, but if we were to build homes and establish industries in other parts of the country. There is nothing further I wish to say in this connection, Mr. Speaker.
