speechtext:
The
question raised by the hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy) is one in which
1390	HOUSE OF
Housing-Sales to Veterans I have also some interest. In the city of Cranbrook in British Columbia Central Mortgage and Housing, in the same year 1948, undertook a similar venture on behalf of the veterans. I had the privilege of visiting these homes at the request of the residents who were expecting to purchase. I must confess that I found conditions similar to those outlined by the hon. member for York South. These houses were built by mass production methods and at a time when materials were somewhat difficult to obtain, and some poor materials were put into the houses. Many of the door latches would not keep the doors closed. While there were doors on cupboards, they tended to sag and would not stay closed.
I inquired of various contractors as well as one or two people who were in the real estate business, and they felt that because of the nature of these homes there was a tendency towards a devaluation of the entire area in which they were built. These houses were built for low rental purposes in an area set aside for that purpose. It is feared by those who are purchasing them that when they put up $7,000 or $8,000 for a home and spend additional money to put it in the condition in which they wish to have it, it would be difficult for them to get their equity returned if for any reason they were forced to sell the house.
It seemed to be the general opinion, therefore, that the houses were being offered at between $500 and $1,000 more than their actual value. I am not a contractor or a real estate agent, so I could not say definitely that this is true. It was my considered opinion that they were being offered at too high a figure.
There is another point in respect of this proposed sale in that if the tenant resides in the home for five years, Central Mortgage and Housing is prepared to reduce the price by $1,000. I know it is the hope and the intention of Central Mortgage and Housing as well as the policy of the government that people should own their own homes. We are encouraging such a policy. However, I feel that if an individual wishes to make an investment it is not our business to tell him that he should own this home or that. If he has had the privilege for a few years of home ownership, and if he wishes to sell and return to a rental basis, that is his own business.
I feel that the price of the house should be set as near as possible to the cost, without reference to how many years the tenant may live in it. Some attempt should be made by the minister to assure the veterans that if the price must be the price that has been asked, the actual cost of the entire program to Central Mortgage and Housing would be


shown. I attended a meeting of the veterans affected and they felt the price being asked was very much in excess of the actual cost. Of course it is the policy of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation when making sales-and perhaps it is a good business practice-not to give the actual cost, or to relate the sales price to that cost. Certainly a real estate agent does not make all these factors known. He simply sets the price and leaves it up to the purchaser to decide whether he is getting full value.
However, in view of the fact that this is a veterans' project and was carried out on behalf of the veterans, I think a better explanation should be given. If at all possible the prices of these houses should be reduced so as to be more in line with the wishes of the veterans concerned.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert H. Winters (Minister of Public Works):
subtopic: SALES TO VETERANS IN HAMILTON AND PETERBOROUGH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy) for providing me with an opportunity to say a few words on this matter which, obviously, has been causing some concern to veterans, particularly those referred to in Peterborough and Hamilton. This subject has come before the house on other occasions.
I am grateful, too, for the contributions made by the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks) and the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Byrne). I do not intend to take up much time in debating the matter, but I think it would be helpful if I placed before hon. members certain salient facts about these houses and their terms of sale.
As hon. members know, quite a number of houses have been built by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation for veterans. There is also a program now under way in which the Department of Veterans Affairs and Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation co-operate to provide houses for veterans. I think both departments have approached housing for veterans in a most sympathetic manner, and I would hope that the majority of hon. members would agree with that statement.
These houses generally are divided into two vintages, those built prior to 1948 and those built subsequent to 1948. The ones built prior to 1948 were put into a sales position at a lower selling price than those built in 1948 and 1949; and for obvious reasons. In the first place, they are older; second, they were built at a time when construction costs were less. Third, most of them have no basements, whereas those built in 1948 and 1949 were constructed under National Housing Act standards. Most of them are pretty good houses, with basements.

There are about 12,000 houses in the 1948-49 vintage which have been put up for sale by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation at the request of veterans who either occupied the houses or who, for one reason or another, had an interest in them. Within the corporation we debated at some length as to just what the government's position should be regarding making these houses available for sale. So long as the conflict was current in Korea we felt we did have an obligation to retain a pool of rental housing for veterans who would be returning from that conflict. On the other hand we felt that we should have regard to the many requests on the part of veterans to make these houses available to them on a permanent basis.
We have now put these houses in what Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation describes as a sales position. We have tried to establish the sales prices so that on an over-all national basis they would be available to veterans at cost. There is no attempt on the part of the corporation to make a profit out of this operation.
Then the hon. member for York South referred to the particular projects at Peterborough and Hamilton. I understand there are some 326 houses at Peterborough, of which 20 have now been sold; and there are 117 at Hamilton of which 10 have been sold, and all to veterans. Non-veterans are not eligible to buy these houses.
The hon. member pointed to the fact that the houses do not appear to be moving very fast, because not many of them have been sold. In reply I would say that no sales promotion is being undertaken here. We leave it to the veteran to decide whether he wants to buy a house or does not want to buy it. It is not something the government is trying to push.
The average selling price in Peterborough is $7,483; the average selling price in Hamilton is $7,562. There are some factors which make it appear that the price at which a house is being offered to a veteran is higher than it really is. In the first place, when these houses were built there was an agreement with the municipality under which they put up about $600 for servicing. Under the terms of the agreement with the municipality that amount must now be repaid to it, and this of course is being recovered out of the sales price of the house.
On the other hand it was recognized that the houses are being made available to veterans at less than the normal market price in the area. We did not want to see speculation and trafficking in these houses
Marpole Bridge
which, we hoped, would be retained by veterans who needed and wanted them. With that in mind Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation devised the formula referred to by the hon. member for York South and the hon. member for Kootenay East, of charging initially $1,000 more than the ultimate price to the buyer if he continued to occupy the house for a minimum period of five years. If that is the case he does not pay that thousand dollars in the purchase price.
These houses are being made available on a basis that in my opinion is fair and equitable. They put up only 10 per cent as a down payment. The balance is paid over a period of 25 years, on the average, at normal National Housing Act rates of interest.
I think those are the essential facts of the case. There is no effort whatever by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to make a profit. These houses are being made available on a basis that, over-all, nationally speaking, will return costs to the corporation and nothing more. There is no effort to sponsor a sales drive to get the houses into the hands of veterans. They were put into a sales position only because it was our understanding that veterans across the country wished the opportunity to buy the houses. I think the deal is a good one; and I hope a majority of members and of veterans agree with me.

Mr. Speaker, there is one question I should like to place before the house briefly this afternoon. It has to do with the Marpole bridge, about which hon. members have heard on different occasions. At the present time, of course, there is a very old bridge over the north arm of the Fraser river which is the only means of access to the international airport on Sea island. There has been a great deal of discussion about the construction of a new bridge, and the province has asked that the dominion should pay one-third of the cost, failing which the province itself would build a bridge and put it on a toll basis. I would ask the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Winters) to clarify the stand of the dominion government today concerning this bridge.
On February 3 the minister answered a question which had been asked by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Mac-Innis) about the policy of the dominion as to sharing in the cost of a bridge. The question and answer are to be found on page 793 of Hansard. Then the hon. member for

Marpole Bridge
Burnaby-Richmond (Mr. Goode) asked a supplementary question which brought this reply from the minister:
That offer was based upon the federal government's interest in having traffic proceed with the greatest facility between the mainland of Vancouver and Sea island. This present Oak street project involves a new large bridge from Vancouver to Lulu island and another smaller bridge from Lulu island to Sea island. To the extent that this new project is in keeping with the federal government's aim in making the $400,000 offer, I assume it will be available for this new project.
That seemed to be a clear commitment to pay $400,000 toward the cost of a new bridge; but the following day a dispatch appeared in the Vancouver Province which read as though the minister did not mean quite what was said in the answer the previous day. I hold in my hand the dispatch which contains this paragraph:
Outside the house, he said-
That is referring to the Minister of Public Works.
-in an interview a condition of federal participation also will be that no tolls are charged on the bridge.
The day before the minister had not said that if the provincial government levied a toll on traffic over this new bridge the dominion would not make a contribution of even $400,000. That point was not made clear by the minister, but in the interview with the correspondent of the Vancouver Daily Province he appeared to take the stand that the federal government would not pay one cent if the provincial government charged a toll on traffic over the bridge.
This stand with regard to tolls had been taken by the Minister of Public Works previously, according to a press dispatch of December 11 of last year, in which he is quoted as saying:
"Under some circumstances," said Mr. Winters, "we might still have been ready to contribute the $400,000 to the larger project planned by the province, but we obviously cannot contribute to a revenue producing project." (The new span is likely to be a toll bridge).
Of course, the tolls are to be levied only until the cost of the bridge has been collected. It is not a matter of the provincial government making money out of the tolls. It merely levies a toll on traffic until the bridge has been paid for. The people who will be using this new bridge will now be in this position. The provincial government is going to build a high-level bridge, and presumably the dominion government will not make any contribution whatever. Therefore the people will have to pay tolls until the whole cost of that bridge has been met.
I ask the Minister of Public Works just what the position of the dominion is today

with regard to this bridge. I also repeat my submission to the minister that the dominion government should pay one-third of the cost of the high-level bridge. The figure of $400,000 which he mentioned was based merely on putting a lift span in the centre of the old bridge. That would mean the bridge would have to open just as often with the lift span as it does with the swing span which is there at the present time. It would mean that the bridge would be opened betwen 6,000 and 7,000 times in a year. Those were the approximate figures. Every little tug that comes up the north arm of the Fraser blows its whistle and the bridge has to open; and that is a terrible inconvenience. It interferes with the only means of access to the greatest airport in Canada. The situation is nothing short of tragic.
I do submit that the dominion should pay its share. It would mean the payment of about $3 million. The total cost of the bridge is expected to be something under $10 million. I believe that tenders for part of the work have already been received and opened by the provincial government, and they are considerably lower than had been expected.
Conferences have been held here in Ottawa between the Minister of Public Works of the dominion and the minister for the province. The latter is Mr. Philip A. Gaglardi. The story of the conferences was summarized in the Vancouver Province last week in an article right across a full page. On one side is a picture of the Minister of Public Works entitled "Bob". On the other side is a picture of the minister of public works of British Columbia entitled "Phil". In the middle is a picture of the old Marpole bridge. The heading reads:
Beautiful friendship fades. Phil and Bob get their spans crossed. An invitation to go fishing falls flat.
One has only to refer to the return brought down by the Minister of Public Works containing the correspondence between himself and the British Columbia minister to realize just how accurate this summary made by the Province reporter last week actually is. For example, there is the first letter, dated March 25, from Victoria addressed to the Hon. Mr. Winters from Mr. Gaglardi. It begins:
I am sending to you under separate cover, a copy of the proposed Oak street bridge plan-
This is the plan for the $10 million bridge. The letter goes on:
-which was presented to me in February of 1954 by Phillips, Barratt and Partners who are consulting engineers in the city of Vancouver, which I am sure you will find to be very interesting.
Along with this I am sending you photostatic copies of newspapers which carried the story of

the information that the federal government was definitely going to help with at least one-third of the share of the building of this proposed bridge.
And I emphasize the word "this".
The last paragraph reads as follows:
Thanking you again for your kind consideration. Best personal regards. Don't forget that fishing trip out this way some time this summer.
On April 28 Mr. Gaglardi wrote again to the Minister of Public Works as follows:
Further to our conversation of yesterday-
Apparently the two ministers had an interview on the 27th.
-I would like to make our position clear as to what is meant by one-third of the cost of the replacing of the Marpole bridge. Remember I mentioned that it would be necessary for a crossing of the Moray channel as well which is all contained in the submission sent to you that was prepared by Phillips, Barratt and Partners.
This seems to show that the Minister of Public Works here in Ottawa was clearly told just what the provincial government had in mind. I now come to the letter of May 11 from the provincial minister, which reads as follows:
Further to our conversation of April 27, I wish to make a formal application for federal participation of one-third of the cost of the proposed Oak street bridge system which will replace the Marpole bridge. When I mention Oak street bridge system,
I mean the bridge across the north arm of the Fraser river and also Moray channel as a direct line between Lulu island and Sea island.
My understanding of the conversation with you was, if the provincial government would be willing to contribute one-third of the cost of the Vesuvius bay and Crofton project, you would be willing to commit the federal government to a one-third share of the above named projects, namely Oak street bridge and the crossing of the Moray [DOT]channel.
The dominion Minister of Public Works replied to that letter on May 14 by a letter which seems to me rather surprising. He said:
Further to our recent conversation, I am pleased to be able to inform you that the federal government is prepared to participate in the cost of a bridge to replace the present and inadequate .Marpole bridge.
The minister himself admits it is inadequate.
I understand it was estimated some time ago that a suitable bridge with a lift span-
That is simply a span in the old bridge.
-would cost $1,200,000 and that Mr. Howe and perhaps others of my colleagues intimated that because of the nature of the Vancouver airport and the fact that it is relatively isolated on an island-Sea island-there was some reason for federal government participation. I believe it was intimated further that the federal government might be expected to contribute one-third of the cost. On this basis, I am authorized to inform you that the federal government is prepared to pay one-third of the cost of a suitable bridge to replace the present Marpole bridge, with a maximum ;participation of $400,000.
Marpole Bridge
For the first time the minister here brings up this question of a maximum of $400,000. That just about queered the fishing trip. Then we have a letter from the British Columbia minister dated June 1, 1954 in which he says:
In reply to your letter of May 14, I first want to say that I am at a complete loss as to what brought about your decision with regard to the proposition I placed before you. While in conversation with you at my recent visit, you understood clearly that I was talking about the Oak street bridge as a replacement to the old Marpole bridge. Any suggestion that a lift span a little bit higher than the present one would be an adequate replacement is met with tremendous ridicule here, and rightly so. At a crucial time when traffic would be trying to make the airport for plane appointments, there is no guarantee that a boat the size necessitating the span to be open would not be travelling on the river, so the bottleneck would in no wise be eliminated.
I have every confidence in your sincerity, and know that when I was discussing this with you, your understanding was the same as mine. We were talking about replacing the Marpole bridge with the Oak street bridge, and your promise to me was that if I would ask my government to look with favour on a third participation in the Vesuvius bay-Crofton ferry wharves which entails approximately $30,000, you would ask your government for a third of the Oak street and Moray channel bridges, which would involve close to $3,000,000.
Then there is a letter from the dominion minister dated July 8, 1954, in which he says that the minister of public works of British Columbia has made a big mistake. This letter contains this paragraph:
When we talked about this matter in Ottawa, the only point of discussion was the replacement of the Marpole bridge. You apparently regarded the Oak street bridge as a replacement for the Marpole bridge whereas I, in fact, never did take any such view.
It looks as though the two ministers were talking more about fishing than about bridges, because their minds do not seem to have met at all, judging by this correspondence. Then on July 13, 1954, there follows a letter from the British Columbia minister which reads:
I wish to acknowledge your letter of July 8 re the Marpole bridge and thank you very much for same. It is true that the meaning I took from our conversation was that the building of the new Oak street bridge would be a replacement of the Marpole bridge. I wish to say I accept your explanation but still feel that in all fairness you must consider one-third portion of the building of the Oak street bridge. Remember that the federal government gave 50 per cent to the provincial government for the building of the highway from Victoria to the Pat bay airport. This bridge will serve the Vancouver airport and I do not see why it is unreasonable that the federal government should be expected to pay one-third.
I will have to visit Ottawa again and wish to spend some more time talking to you about this bridge. In the meantime, if you are coming out west, let me know. I still want to take you on that fishing trip.

Marpole Bridge
Then follows other correspondence, but the next letter which is material is one from the Minister of Public Works dated October 28, 1954, in which he refers to the $400,000. The letter reads:
On May 14, 1954, I wrote, Informing you that the government had agreed to participate in the cost of a bridge to replace the present Marpole bridge up to one-third of the cost of the new structure, to a maximum of $400,000. To date, we have received no indication of whether the government of British Columbia intends to avail itself of this offer.
I am now in the process of preparing the estimates of the Department of Public Works for the oncoming fiscal year, 1955-56. Since you have not indicated that the above amount, in whole or in part, will be required next year, I thought X should inform you that I am not including in my estimates an item for this project. However, the federal government's readiness to participate still stands. In the event that your government wishes to have us share in the project to the above-mentioned extent, please let me know and I will take the necessary steps to have the required amount of money made available at the appropriate time.
Then we have a letter dated December 7, 1954, from the Minister of Public Works to the Richmond board of trade which had written asking that the dominion contribute one-third. The minister states:
Although there is no direct federal responsibility, the government was impressed by the unique traffic situation which obtains between the mainland and the airport on Sea island. Parliament accordingly authorized this department-
That of course was a mistake because parliament had not authorized anything. It was the minister who was promising these things.
Parliament approved a vote last year.
I do not think a vote was ever put through for $400,000.

It was discussed on the
estimates last year.

I may be wrong. I wish the minister would check that, as I do not think he is right. The letter continues:
Parliament accordingly authorized this department to participate in the cost of constructing a bridge to replace the present Marpole bridge up to an amount of $400,000.
Then there is another letter dated December 7, 1954 from the minister to the international association of machinists, one paragraph of which reads:
The question of whether tolls should, or should not be charged, is entirely one for the provincial government, and I presume they are prepared to exercise their responsibility with respect to it.
There is no suggestion there that if tolls were to be charged the government would not put up $400,000. There is a final letter

from the minister of public works of British Columbia dated December 17, 1954, which reads in part:
I know that you realize I cannot agree with what you have to say and know that you also realize that this is definitely a federal responsibility. I am hoping and praying that the day will come prior to this bridge being open, when the federal government will see that it has a definite responsibility here in helping us to build this structure so that no tolls will be necessary.
I feel that this matter has not by any means been concluded, and that in your own capable manner you will think this situation over more thoroughly and some day come up with the offer of the one-third for which I feel the federal government is very much responsible.
The Province reporter ends his dispatch with a summary of the situation, after referring to the letter I have just read, as follows:
So the matter rests. Ottawa still has $400,000 that says it will help build a (non-toll) bridge at Marpole. Victoria is building at Oak street and blaming Ottawa for the tolls.
Maybe when the bridge is built Bob and Phil will both fish off it-for votes.

Mr. Speaker, when I adjourned the debate on Friday evening I had been saying I considered that the government had been somewhat dilatory in its present avowed intention of bringing to an end this matter of deceitful packaging. This bill concerns something which, in a domestic way, is of interest to all of us. It might be considered a somewhat trivial matter, but I think people who are using consumer goods should have some guarantee that, when they buy something, it will have some conformity to the advertising and to the packaging. I refer, of course, to the packaging of bacon.
The housewife is concerned with the leanness of bacon. I think it is fairly well known to most of us that the fat in bacon disappears in the frying pan and to all intents and purposes is lost. The housewife can buy lard in a different form of package much more cheaply than she can buy prime bacon. She is looking for bacon, not for lard; but she is paying for the lard the same price which she would expect to pay for the prime bacon. She does not want to buy a pig in a poke, but I must say that is exactly what she is doing. The manufacturer sees to it that the poke is well sealed up so she cannot get her fingers inside it or get a look to see what the contents are really like.
That is the first thing to which I object. The second and perhaps also trifling matter was explained to us I think by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin), among others, namely the method by which this bacon is laid in rows in such a system that the lean and not the fat is shown. The third and the most objectionable feature-the one to which I violently object-is the deceitful use on the package itself of red lines which make of it a facsimile of the leaner meat which the housewife desires and which she wants to purchase.
My hon. friend who raised this question in the form of this draft bill-and I congratulate

Food and Drugs Act
him upon raising the matter-and the Minister of National Health and Welfare discussed the legal aspects. In his speech at page 1304 of Hansard the minister used the following words:
I shall take the position, of course, as my hon. friend has anticipated, that the law as it stands at present is adequate to deal with this particular problem;
Later on the same page he is reported as follows:
I shall readily admit at once that it is a practice which cannot, under any circumstances, be condoned.
It is in view of those statements that I suggest to the government that it has been somewhat dilatory in acting. As a matter of fact it has not acted at all. I consider it might have acted forthrightly upon the matter.
Some time ago I saw a news clipping which stated that the government-I presume the minister's department-had issued some sort of directive or had given a piece of advice to the packing companies. The minister has assured us that it is his opinion that this practice, as a result of that warning or advice, will now cease. As reported at page 1305 of Hansard the minister stated:
But I may tell my hon. friend that we have issued a directive to the trade telling them that in our judgment this practice is not valid, that it is not legitimate under the act, and must be stopped.
I point out to the minister and to the house, however, that in spite of that directive deceptively packaged bacon is still on the counters of the stores. The fact that the government has been dilatory in putting a stop to this practice is proved by another fact, namely that this packaging has been going on for a long time. In spite of the minister's assertion that the present laws, without amendment, are sufficient to cope with and stop that practice, apparently the trade does not agree with him. If it knows the law it certainly displays a complete confidence that that law will not be enforced. It is apparently right in that assumption, because this matter was brought to the attention of this house and of the government years ago. The trade is apparently willing to take a chance upon the enforcement of the legislation in order to maintain its own profits. I think something stronger than a directive is necessary to remedy the situation.
As I have said, this protest now raised by the hon. member for Kamloops is not by any means a new thing. Some hon. members may or may not recall that I myself raised the matter away back in 1949. To be precise, I raised it on September 30, 1949. If hon. members refer to Hansard of that date they

will find the debate that ensued on the subject. I raised the matter upon the estimates of the Department of Agriculture when the minister was in his seat.
On that occasion I said, if I may paraphrase a few of my own words, that I had no objection to the packaging of bacon in cellophane if the housewife found it handier in that form and if she was willing to pay the extra expense. By the way, there is a good deal of extra expense involved. You cannot handle these bacon strips and package them for nothing. I have no objection to a cellophane package through which you can see clearly, but at that time I objected to the red streaking. I considered that the borderline had been crossed between honesty and deceit. Caveat emptor, let the buyer beware, is I suppose a good admonition to give anyone in any case, but it becomes a more vital admonition in view of certain modern commercial practices. It was an extremely useful admonition in a horse trade, but at least when you were buying a horse you could see his blemishes. You certainly did not expect to have those blemishes covered up by paint which was the same colour as the hair of the horse.
At the time of that debate the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) did not appear to take the matter too seriously. Here is what he said, and I quote from page 421 of Hansard of September 30, 1949, under the name of the Minister of Agriculture:
The hon. member referred to the bacon wrappers.
Then he said he did not know much about it, and went on to say:
However, I do notice that often it is in these wrapped packages and I notice also that that is true right across the country. I suppose those who have the product for sale are trying to put it up in the form in which people are most likely to buy it. If somebody in Canada Packers has made a mistake in the type of package they are using, if it does not suit the public, then I presume it will not be very long before Burns or Swifts will find that out and put out some other form of package. In any case the public buys it.
I suggest that is a pretty specious argument, and that is just the thing with which I am finding fault, that the public does buy it because it is deceitfully packaged. I have seen women at counters where there was a slab of bacon and they could clearly see the proportion of fat and lean. They would take a look at it, and then deliberately go over to another counter, take one of these red packages of what looked like completely lean bacon, and discover later that once again they had made a mistake. I do not know whether or not they discovered their mistake, but I shall not enter into that. The Minister of Agriculture then went on to say:
The hon. member wants to know who has control over this. In so far as the last few weeks

or possibly months are concerned, this government certainly would have no control or at the most very little. We have not been able to get any bacon to send out of the country___
This of course applied to the time immediately after the war.
and our control is confined to the regulation of products in international or interprovincial trade. There is very little bacon crossing even the provincial boundaries at the present time as most of the bacon produced is consumed in the province where it is produced. Therefore the control would be entirely with the provinces.
You will notice, as I said, that argument of the Minister of Agriculture scarcely holds water when he says that the red lining on bacon packages promotes sales. Of course the packers put up the bacon in a form which is most likely to induce the public to buy it. That is why they do it, to get the public to buy inferior meat, from the point of view of fat content, at an enhanced price.
The women of the country have been concerned about this practice for a long time. As a matter of fact, I remember that the reason I raised the question in 1949 was that I had had a circular letter from the Canadian Association of Consumers who were airing their grievances in that regard. At the same time they wrote to us as members of parliament they sent out a questionnaire, presumably to their members or perhaps to the general public, I do not know, in which they asked certain questions. The answers would appear to contradict the minister's opinion as to the popularity of this particular product. I quote now from the foot of page 420 of Hansard of the same date. One of the questions was:
What Is your opinion of the red and white striped bacon wrapping?
The opinions were compiled as follows:
(a)	Over 61 per cent thought it deceiving.
(b)	About 15 per cent were indifferent or had not noticed that type of wrapping.
(c)	About 2 per cent preferred that type of wrapping.
(d)	Less than 2 per cent thought it better quality.
(e)	Over 19 per cent stated they preferred plain wrapping.
Along with the answers to the questions there were a good many comments with regard to this method of using a red striped package for bacon, a few of which I shall put on the record. Some of the comments were:
Misleading and annoying, deceptive, too much fat, think they are trying to fool the buyer-
May I interject that I am afraid they do. -the dye comes off, detracting to quality, a snare and a delusion, taints the meat, looks messy, keeps too moist and hastens molding, silly and unnecessary, takes the clerk's time opening it up to show the customer-
Food and Drugs Act
Of course, nous avons change tout cela. Now they do not open it any more, as I have explained.
-eye appeal and draws the crowd.
That is the case, and it is my case for saying that if the minister is correct in his assertion that the present legislation, which I presume was legislation that was passed previous to these complaints-

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: No, it was brought in later. It was brought in during the session before last.
The minister may be right.
I am right. My hon. friend will remember that we brought in a revision of the Food and Drugs Act two years ago.
Can the minister tell me about when the new legislation was introduced?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: The session before last, and it was proclaimed last June.
That would be a couple of years ago.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: It was proclaimed last June.

I am not going to quiz the minister about why it was not proclaimed earlier, but my assertion is that in view of the fact that the practice has been in effect all these years, in view of the fact that the matter was raised in the house in 1949, and in view of the statement of the minister that the practice is objectionable, cannot be condoned and must be stopped, it might have been stopped before now. I do not know whether the minister will agree that would be a reasonable conclusion to which I might come.
The minister says the government now has the power to stop it. He is optimistic, perhaps, when he suggests that this warning on the part of the government may have some effect.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: It is a directive.
There is a difference between a directive and a warning. My legal education is improving all the time. But I suggest that now the government has the power it should stop the practice forthwith.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Has my hon. friend given any consideration to the legal implications of how you stop it?

I have given some thought to it, and I heard the hon. member for Kamloops and the minister discuss that matter when .the bill was last before the house. Whether or not I am much wiser, I am not prepared to say.

Oh, I think we grow wiser with each hour.

Mr. Speaker, I am not here to defend the bacon processors, nor to defend the use of red stripes on bacon packages. I know something about the processing and sale of bacon, and I feel I should say something on the subject.
There is no doubt about the purpose of the red lines on the bacon wrapping. They were put there to enhance the appearance of the bacon, and to sell more bacon. That is quite evident. Some smart aleck started this practice several years ago and all the packers were forced to follow suit or their bacon would remain on the counters and never be picked up. Therefore one can see that the very ladies who have complained about the practice are the people who pick up the packages with the red lines and leave the packages without the red lines lying there unsold.
I doubt whether there are many ladies who are misled by the red lines on the package. I have spoken to several of them and they have said, "You are not kidding me about it; you have not fooled me on that subject at all". The hon. member for Kamloops bewails this despicable practice-I do not like that word-but he neglects to mention the many cases where artificial colouring is used and mixed right into the product. The bacon wrapper is printed, and the printing does not come off on the food. It does not affect the food in any way. We have so many highly artificial colourings used in icings and in cakes and candies. Then we have the bright red colouring applied to the delicious and justly famous lake Winnipeg goldeye. I do not hear anybody complaining about that, and that is right in the food. Why do we never see a green orange as we did in the past? They are all coloured. A basket of peaches is covered by red netting, as we all know. I believe the practice has been banned in Ontario, but it still prevails in some of the provinces. I do not hear anything about the misleading practice of packaging smoked kippers in bright orange cellophane.
The meat packing industry does not use one ounce of artificial colouring in any meat product. I wish we could say the same about a lot of other foods. We do not hear anything about the colouring of butter. This practice is followed all the time, and the colouring is right in the product. When the hon. member for Kamloops was interviewed by those complaining, I wonder if he noticed how much colouring had been used to paint the lily? An article published in the Calgary Daily Herald has received considerable notice. I received a copy of it from Calgary and one from Winnipeg as well.
I got one too.

Perhaps some hon. members have seen this article in the Calgary Daily Herald. It reads in part as follows:
Women, in fact, have established a rocky reputation for being tough about being bamboozled visually in regard to things they wish to acquire. They want to see the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth, preferably in clear cellophane wrapping untouched and uncamouflaged by human hand.
Women, on the other hand, are people who spend staggering millions of their husbands' painfully earned coin every year buying multi-coloured goo and exotic liquids which they smear on their faces, their eyelids, their eyebrows, their lips, their cheeks, their fingernails, behind their ears, and under their arms, and that's about as far as I think I'll go right now.
All of the bacon processors I have interviewed admit that the red line is misleading and they are quite willing to discontinue its use, providing everyone else does. I do not think there is any doubt of that. The minister has assured us that a directive has been sent out. I know all the processors are taking it seriously, but the problem is that hundreds of thousands of dollars are tied up in these expensive cellophane wrappings. It will take about four months to clear these stocks. I assure you, from my knowledge, the practice will be discontinued in about four months.
Recently the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bryce) made a speech in which he discounted the value of our present hog grading system. I would suggest that he would be better occupied in persuading our hog producers to deliver more high grade hogs and much fewer heavy fat hogs than are being delivered. They are a real problem to the processor and the housewife.
I want to close by assuring you that the percentage of rogues is no greater amongst meat packers than amongst any other industry or occupation, including lawyers. I urge that the farmers give us lean hogs, and the processor will give you lean bacon which will need no misleading wrapper.

I have listened with a great deal of interest to the views expressed by the various members who have spoken on Bill No. 8. As a person with over 40 years of experience in the meat business perhaps I could comment on the subject with some degree of intelligence.
So far as the wrapping of bacon is concerned, it is a comparatively new idea. It gained favour, as did other techniques, with the advent of the supermarket and the serve-yourself method of merchandising. There was a time when you could not buy wrapped bacon if you tried, but that was quite a few years ago. At that time the packers, with

their keen appreciation for quality, did guard the first grade quality of their bacon. The first grade was the result of years of experience and experimentation with various types of curing and various degrees of smoking with various types of sawdust-that is what was used in the old days, but I do not know what they use now. As a result a high standard of quality was developed for the first grade bacon.
For years, I do not know how far back, there has always been a first grade and a second grade. Generally speaking the first grade bacon is known as dry cured. The salt, sugar and other ingredients that go to make up the flavour are rubbed in by hand, which results in a much finer texture and a much better flavour. Generally speaking the No. 2 bacon is processed by the brine cure. I can think back to the time when you could not get a bit of fat bacon in the No. 1 grade. The processors were very particular in selecting the sides of pork that went into the processing of that No. 1 bacon. However, things have changed. In the No. 2 bacon, naturally, because it is No. 2, you expect to get a heavier type of bacon with a certain amount of fat.
Generally speaking, I believe you get what you pay for. Perhaps one of the problems in dealing with this striped package-and I do not condone it for a moment-is the desire of the public to obtain something a little cheaper than they do at the corner butcher store. If one looks carefully I believe one can ascertain whether or not the bacon is extremely fat, but we have people who are bargain hunters. Here I should like to pay tribute to the little fellow on the corner who does a good job of serving the people. If you go into his shop and want lean bacon he will get it for you if he has to tear the shop apart to do it.
I am not trying to be too critical, but I want to tell the truth about this business. This practice of using red striped cellophane in the packaging of bacon is perhaps one of the smallest sins of which the packing trade has been guilty. If you are interested in helping the consumer I could give you a few ideas that would perhaps make it a little easier.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Perhaps the only good thing about the stripes is the colour.

That could be. My experience goes back 44 years, and I do not know whether that is a sign of intelligence or stupidity because I have heard it said that all you need to be a successful butcher is a weak mind and a strong back. Up until the last war there seemed to be a reasonable amount of uniformity in the grades. But when the 50433-89i
Food and Drugs Act
last war came along, and there was not too much bacon available, by degrees the packers got a little more reckless in their sense of values, so far as grades were concerned. Under the guise of No. 1 bacon-and I could give the name of the packer, if you wanted it, but I do not think it is necessary-I have paid for bacon that was at least from three and one-half to four inches thick. It came into my shop during the war. This bacon was not properly cured, according to the usually accepted standards either for brine curing or dry curing.
For the sake of speed, or perhaps for some other reason, the packers pumped the brine into that fresh pork. It was not allowed to cure properly. It was then rushed to the smoke house and given the bare minimum of smoking. That bacon was shipped out under the guise of No. 1 bacon. If you brought it into your shop and did not unpack it immediately you would find when it was unpacked that there would be a puddle of brine under the packing case.
What price?

A pretty husky price. That, of course, was the other extreme. But what I have said is as true as the fact that I am standing here, because I have seen it right in my own shop, and I do not make any bones about it. When the supply became more plentiful and rationing was taken off, the packers had to get into a more reasonable spirit of competition, with the result that bacon grades improved. However, even after controls were lifted the packers persisted in delivering substandard bacon in a great number of case*.
Of course there are exceptions. I have had some very good bacon since coming to Ottawa-and I have had some pretty punk stuff, too. Last Saturday, when I was considering speaking on this subject when it came up again, I was a little more tolerant than I am today. In a shop I saw one of our western popular brands but, after looking through two whole packages, I could not find any that I wanted to buy. According to the wrappings it was all No. 1 bacon.
However, that is only one of the small things we have to worry about. I have seen back bacon, wrapped in packages and marked No. 1 brand, that came off sows. It was extremely heavy bacon. They had trimmed the fat off, and had got around the restriction in that respect. Nevertheless, a sow is a sow, wherever you meet it, and all too often we find that kind of product masqueraded as top-notch or No. 1 bacon. I do not think that is right.

Food and Drugs Act
The other day I heard the Minister of National Health and Welfare say he objected to the butcher slicing the bacon and laying it in the case, sunny side up. Well, there must be a certain amount of showmanship in the meat business, the same as anywhere else.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: My complaint was not so much against the butcher, because after listening to my hon. friend I have great respect for butchers. I take it he is a butcher.

A butcher has a certain technique, and his success or reputation in his field is closely connected with his ability to pretty up his products. He does not do it with deception in mind, but he will pretty them up to the point where they have some appeal to the purchasing public. I have been responsible for putting in some fancy fresh meat windows in my day; I have resorted to carving flowers on loins of pork, and the like. I have done many things to enhance the sales value of a particular product, but never once have I done it to deceive.
I believe the wrapping of bacon is not a bad practice. Where would the self-service stores be today if it were not for the wrapping not only of bacon but of everything else?
I agree with much of what the hon. member has said; but can he tell me why the packer has chosen red wrapping when he follows this practice?
Perhaps it is more pleasant to the eye. Generally speaking meat is red in colour.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: It is more pleasing; that is why the Liberal party adopted that colour.

I would hate to think there has been any deliberate planning on the part of the processor. Perhaps the basic idea was to enhance the appearance of the package. The first wrapped bacon I remember was the product of an ambitious salesman who had the idea that it would be a good thing to place on bacon some cellophane wrapping bearing a holly design and a trade name, and also the compliments of a merchant. This was sold with a value equivalent to that of a calendar. Very often in business we gave a customer the choice of the fancy packaged bacon or a calendar. They were worth about the same amount. This was a good stunt, from the standpoint of salesmanship.
At that time one got exactly what he expected-No. 1 bacon, the very best of it. But in that case the covering was more deceptive than the red lines of today, if one wished to look at it in that way. If we want to get right down to the point of being fair

to everybody, I do not think the packing plants should work for nothing, any more than anyone else should. But I do maintain- and I know from experience-that there is altogether too great a discrepancy between the rail grade price of hogs and what we have to pay for pork wholesale. No one can tell me anything different, because I can prove it in many cases. Some consideration should be given to prices at that level. One of the greatest discrepancies is in the merchandising of products.
Under an honest arrangement no one would have to pay $1.02, $1.03, or $1.04 a pound for Canadian ham that had come off a hog priced at 32 cents, rail grade; nor should anyone have to pay 95 cents a pound for back bacon off the same grade of hog. I do not think that is necessary to make a fair margin of profit, and I place everything else in the same category. I have seen bacon at these prices that was not off a select hog supposed to be up to the standard of this 32-cent level I spoke of. I have seen cooked hams brought into my shop that came off that same kind of sow or heavy hog that is supposed to be sold at a two-thirds value as compared with a No. 1 hog.
I want to be fair to the processors and to the consumers. I would suggest that these relative grades be definitely designated so that if a person wants to buy sow-back bacon he can buy it, but at its proper price. I certainly oppose with all the power I possess this system of racketeering so far as price spreads are concerned.
I do not want to delay the house unduly, but these are things that are very important to me. Since Bill No. 8 is designed to safeguard the interests of the consumer I would suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the same principle be carried right across the board and we have a look at every phase of marketing.
I want to say a few words on this bill. I do not suppose it is very controversial, because the minister has already given his moral support to it.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: What I said was that our legislation was better than this particular proposal.
Of course; the minister has already pointed out that the government was doing more effectively the thing that the hon. member for Kamloops is asking to be done.
No.

I would like to point out that this idea of passing laws on such things as beautifying bacon is going a little bit too far. I would hate to see someone bring in a law

next year prohibiting young girls from using lipstick or cosmetics. When I heard the speech of the hon. member for Waterloo North (Mr. Schneider) today I wondered whether he was not giving ideas to those on the other side who seem to have such a mania for bringing in new laws. As far as I am concerned nature knew her business when she made young girls pretty, when she put the red in the right places and the curves in the right places, and if any of the young girls can help nature along I am not going to be the one to say no, so I would not like to see anyone pass a law in that regard.
Since we are on the subject of packaging and cellophane I want to take this occasion to say that in my opinion there is far too much of it. In my opinion one of the great backward movements of this century is the constantly increasing cost of distribution occasioned by these expensive methods of merchandising. They are always getting frills and furbelows on the packaging. When I used to send my shirts out in the old days- when I first started to wear shirts that went to the laundry-I could send them to the Chinese laundry on the corner and I would get them back for a few cents. But now when I send my shirt to the laundry it comes back wrapped in so many layers of coloured cellophane that I am paying as much for the cellophane and the extra packaging and the things I do not want at all as I used to pay for a whole new shirt when I was a boy 50 years ago. I do think that we have gone much too far with all of this fancy merchandising, and it would be a good thing if we got back to the simpler way.
As far as I am concerned, with the pure food act that we have now and an alert administration, together with the fact that we have already been told that the packers themselves are going to take common-sense joint action to see that the suggestion is carried out, I cannot see why anybody should get excited about these little red stripes on the bacon packages. When I listened to the speeches the other day about how the poor women were being deceived all the way down the line, I thought of my own wife. I went back to our own refrigerator and took out a package of bacon to see if anybody could deceive my wife by these little red stripes. I give you my word that certainly no one could deceive my wife by these stripes and get her to pay a single cent extra for the bacon.
In my opinion the great modern supermarkets, with all their high-class merchandising, fancy packages and selling people things
Food and Drugs Act
they never asked for and do not want to buy, are not doing as good a job dollar for dollar and cent for cent as was done by the old corner grocer and corner butcher 50 years ago.
They are doing better.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert H. Winters (Minister of Public Works):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on a question of privilege, I understand that under the rules of the house I am not permitted to speak twice on the same motion and therefore I am prevented from replying to the speech made by the hon. member for Yancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green).
I was not quite finished.

I should like however to deal with my question of privilege. During the course of his speech the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra stated that this offer of $400,000 to which he was referring as the federal government's contribution to a suitable replacement for the existing Marpole bridge had never been approved by parliament. He told the house he believed I was mistaken when I said it had been approved by parliament. I interjected that parliament had approved a vote last year.
I was wrong in that and the hon. member was entirely correct. I had in mind the several times we had discussed this question during the course of the main and supplementary estimates, and my announcement in the house on May 12, 1954. It is a fact that there was no vote as such approved by parliament.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the minister for giving that explanation. I have very little to add to what I said before five o'clock, except that I believe the first intimation that the government would not contribute anything to the construction of the new bridge was at the time of the press interview last December. I checked the minister's statement on May 12, 1954, to be found at page 4645 of Hansard of last session, at which time he made his announcement that the government would contribute $400,000. There was no mention then that the money would not be forthcoming if there were to be tolls charged on traffic over the bridge. Then on June 25 I questioned the parliamentary assistant about this matter, which discussion will be found commencing at page 6774 of Hansard:
