speechtext:
I think the amount of $400,000 has been offered to the province to build the Marpole bridge, but I am informed that they want to build the bridge at Oak street.
IMr. Green.]
Previously, as reported on the same page, I had read a newspaper article which showed that the provincial government was going to charge tolls if the dominion government did not contribute one-third. I had actually read that clipping before the parliamentary assistant made this answer.
That is right.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Public Works
speechtext: So far, I do not think-

Does that mean then that unless the provincial government agrees to this ridiculous scheme of simply putting a lift on the old Marpole bridge, the dominion government will not make any contribution at all?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Public Works
speechtext: I am told that they will probably make the same offer for the Oak street bridge.
The dominion government will pay $400,000 on a new bridge on Oak street?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Public Works
speechtext: That is right, Mr. Chairman.
I hope they will have a further look at it because they are going to have to pay more than that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
I am not making any comment on that statement.
The stand by the government that they will not pay one red cent because the provincial government is proposing to place a toll on the traffic comes very close to breaking a commitment. It certainly is very close to being bad faith. I submit that the dominion government cannot in fairness get out of the contribution which the government itself promised, not only once but many times, not only through the present minister and his parliamentary assistant but before that by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe). If the government fails to carry out that promise it is breaking faith with the people of British Columbia.
Furthermore, I believe the government should pay a full one-third of the cost of the new bridge. Most of the traffic over that bridge will be to and from Vancouver airport. A tremendous amount of air traffic is using that airport, which is also a Royal Canadian Air Force base. The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Campney) explained that just a day or two ago. Everything depends upon access to the island on which the airport is situated. I urge the Minister of Public Works not to withdraw his offer of $400,000, but rather to increase that offer to a full one-third share of the total cost of the new bridge.

Mr. Speaker, several times since coming here in 1949 I have asked the federal government to contribute one-third toward the cost of the Oak street bridge, the reason being, of course, that the approaches to the bridge are in my riding. I have asked three or four times for the production of papers, and the minister has kindly kept me advised on certain negotiations that were going on.
I am very much afraid that the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) is

stating his case and basing it entirely upon newspaper reports. If he had had as much to do with the Oak street bridge as I have he would know that the confusion that was quite evident in the returns I received a few days ago did not represent all the confusion by any means. Because I had supported the provincial government of British Columbia in this matter, some time ago I contacted Mr. Gaglardi, the provincial minister of public works. He knew at that time that I was supporting the provincial government on this one matter. I then asked him what had happened in Ottawa, and his story to me of course was not nearly what the facts bore out in regard to this return.
The matter of this bridge has constituted a long story in British Columbia. It has gone past the point of whether the federal government is going to contribute one-third; it has gone past the point of whether the city of Vancouver is interested. This bridge has become a political matter in connection with the gaining of votes at the next provincial election in British Columbia. Whether or not we like it, that is the situation in my riding.
Some time ago the minister of public works of British Columbia spoke to the board of trade in Richmond. This was in the spring of 1954. He told that very august body that the detailed plans and specifications for this bridge were in Ottawa, that the Minister of Public Works knew of the plans and the estimated cost. He told my people that in open meeting, and it was reported in the press. The federal Minister of Public Works indicated that those remarks were not quite correct, because the plans for the Oak street bridge did not arrive here in detail until I think November, 1954, even though it had been reported many times in the British Columbia press that our Minister of Public Works was fully informed of the facts and figures regarding the bridge. I do not blame the Minister of Public Works if he is confused on the issue. I have been in on the top planning of this bridge for many months and I am confused, as are the people I represent.
A number of veterans in my riding have their property under expropriation in connection with the approaches to the bridge. No one in Richmond knows where those approaches are going. The council has not been able to tell the people of my riding the plans for the bridge, where the highway is going and where the southern approaches will be. How can you blame the minister of the federal government if he is confused, when my people who are right there where the bridge is going to be know nothing about it?
Marpole Bridge
About three weeks ago veterans in my riding were given three months to move out of their homes. No explanation was given, nor were they told they were going to get reasonable prices for their property. They were just told that they would have to be out on March 31, under the orders of the British Columbia government. Perhaps the house will remember that the other day I questioned the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Lapointe) in regard to this matter, and his parliamentary assistant said that the veterans would be amply protected by the federal government. This has lifted a load off a lot of little people.
Now the British Columbia government, without consulting this government fully and before the negotiations were even considered completed, has called for tenders on the bridge. The Minister of Public Works expressed some surprise in this house at one time that they would have gone to tender before all negotiations were completed. Now those estimates are in the papers at home. We still do not know in Richmond exactly where the bridge is going. We do not know whether more of the little homes in Richmond are going to be expropriated. It does not seem to matter what the people of Richmond think; all that seems to matter is that an Oak street bridge be built at a considerable cost to the people of British Columbia, without the negotiations being completed either with this government or with the city of Vancouver.
It was the story about a year ago that this was going to be a three-way deal. I remember discussing with certain officials of the provincial government the fact that they were going to ask the city of Vancouver for quite an amount of money. If I remember aright, the city of Vancouver offered $200,000. The minister of public works in our provincial government said that was peanuts. We cannot blame the federal government, much as I should like to in this case because it would be good politics for me. It certainly would be good politics at home; it would gain me many votes if I could just rise and say that the minister of public works in the British Columbia government had been absolutely frank with our minister here. But he has not been frank with him any more than he has been frank with me. I have told him that I have supported his government because, if hon. members will recall it, I said I thought they were sincere. I believed they were going to build a bridge, but I think we are going to fight the building of that bridge in every constituency in British Columbia at the next provincial election.

Marpole Bridge
I have made this statement in my riding and I make it again now. I do not think the British Columbia government want any money from the federal government in connection with this project. I think they are most happy that they cannot make a deal with our minister here, because I can imagine the Social Credit members going throughout the province of British Columbia trying to tell the people that the federal government have refused to give any money toward this bridge, something which is not true.
Are you lining up speeches for us?

You need somebody to line them up. I believe that even now, without consultation with our minister, if British Columbia were to come down here with plans and specifications, and if they were to lay down the whole agreement as it should be laid down, in a sincere and businesslike way, they still could receive a fairly friendly reception. I do not know that they would get any more than $400,000. However, I think their case should be prepared and presented a great deal better than it has been.
What kind of business is this when the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra rises in his place and mentions a return that I asked for in the house the other day, with confusion between two ministers that is quite evident in those papers? What provincial minister ever came to Ottawa to try to sell a bill of goods and left the confusion in the mind of the federal minister that evidently is there now, with the two ministers talking about entirely different things? Does it sound right in this house that a provincial minister should come down here to get $3 million, and these letters are the result? Certainly I can only think my idea that they do not want any federal money is only too true.
The position at the Oak street bridge is this. We have always had the old Marpole bridge. We know that the thing should have been pulled down years ago, but it is there and it is being used every day. We also have another bridge on the other side of Oak street that connects the city of Vancouver with my riding. It is called the Fraser street bridge. Both are freeways. There has never been a toll on them as far as I know, and I do not expect there ever will be.
What is going to be the position here? We are going to put up an Oak street bridge at an annual cost of some $420,000 for interest and maintenance. We are going to have two free bridges, one on each side of it, and yet we are going to charge tolls on the big one. Whoever heard of a proposition like that? Nowhere in British Columbia

has a freeway been taken that has had nothing to do with railways, and another bridge opened in its place with toll charges. I have made the statement at home that the veterans on Sea island, of whom there are some 6,000 or 7,000 to whom the federal government pay family allowances every month, are going to have those family allowances taken away from them because they will have to pay tolls to the government of British Columbia in order to go to work and come home at night. None of us from British Columbia want that. I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that even now it is not too late for the provincial minister to come to Ottawa and talk this matter over in a businesslike way, not in the way that it evidently has been talked over in other visits.
I should like to bring another matter to your attention at the same time, Mr. Speaker. The people of Richmond have been told that because of the federal assessment in Richmond and Sea island, which runs into some millions of dollars, the federal government have an interest there and that, because of that interest, we should put up $3 or $4 million with respect to the Oak street bridge. Not too many weeks ago the government of British Columbia bought the First Narrows bridge in Vancouver. They have also suggested-and I believe they have an inquiry under way at the present time-that they are going to put up another bridge across Bur-rard inlet. Those bridges will cost between $12 and $15 million in total.
Although they try to sell us the idea that the assessment of Richmond and Sea island is a basis for federal contribution to the Oak street bridge, I have information on my desk showing that the assessment in North Vancouver-and the city of Vancouver and the city of North Vancouver are connected by the First Narrows bridge-is almost equal to the assessment of Richmond and Sea island. Yet the provincial government have not asked for a nickel in helping them to finance the First Narrows bridge. Evidently there is one situation on one side of Burrard inlet and another situation on the other side.
But I can view this matter from a different angle. A couple of years ago the federal government tried to buy the airport on Sea island for something over $1 million. Because of a plebiscite in the city of Vancouver that agreement failed. Today the city of Vancouver still owns the Vancouver international airport. I think they are coming around to the position now where they will most likely, in the next few months, offer it to the federal government. I hope they do so, because I do not think cities have any right to the ownership of a large international airport of that

kind. If the airport comes into federal hands I believe this government will have a much greater interest in the Oak street bridge than $400,000.
I would certainly ask the Minister of Public Works to invite the provincial minister here again. We perform no service to our people if we argue by means of letters on a confused issue, as is being done now; whereas if Mr. Gaglardi comes down to Ottawa again and he has his story straight, I do not doubt that our minister here will talk the matter over with him again and perhaps propose some better agreement to his colleagues in the cabinet.
I rather think a larger contribution to this bridge is not too impossible. Because of the fact that we have large military installations at the airport and a large transport assessment in Richmond, it seems to me that $400,000 is a rather small figure for our interest in that part of the country. I hope this meeting will take place, but I suggest that there certainly should be present at that meeting someone from the city of Vancouver who holds some responsibility in this matter. It seems strange to me that the government of British Columbia should have forgotten about the interests of the city of Vancouver lately.
The three parties have an interest, and I think if the city of Vancouver could come forward with about $350,000 or a little more the federal government should consider making a one-third contribution. However, it is not quite as easy as the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra made out this afternoon. He has been a great exponent of the Oak street bridge. I think the people of Vancouver are indebted to him for his efforts, as I hope they are to me. I have tried to present the matter in the most businesslike way I could, and I still ask the minister to take another look at it.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in my view it is time the house heard about another bridge, and that is my reason for rising for a few moments in this debate. I was sorry I had not made sure that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) had seen a certain dispatch in the press before I asked him a question on the orders of the day this afternoon, but I thought he would have seen it. Perhaps I might tell him now that my question was based on a dispatch in this morning's Toronto Globe and Mail which was datelined from Montreal. The heading of the article reads, "Jodoin Suggests 50433-90
Disraeli Bridge
Three-way Parley to Provide Jobs." I should like to read a sentence or two from the article. It reads:
The president of the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada today called for a conference of labour, management and government to help solve unemployment. Claude Jodoin, head of the 580,000-member body, told the Canadian Club the conference should be held immediately to find ways of solving the "terrifying problems of 600,000 unemployed Canadians".
I invite the minister to read the dispatch in full, and perhaps he might be able to comment on it either during this debate tonight or tomorrow on motions or on the orders of the day.
It is also a matter of interest to me that at the same time that one reads that dispatch from Montreal calling for an attack on the problem of unemployment one also finds in today's issue of the Montreal Gazette an article entitled, "Two Tunnels, Two Bridges, said Need." The first paragraph of this article reads:
Montreal plans to ask the federal government to build four new traffic links between Montreal and the south shore at a cost of about $100 million.
Thus you have from the west coast in the matter that has just been under discussion, namely the Marpole bridge, and from Montreal in the dispatch I have just read, an indication that there is a growing feeling in the country that something needs to be done regarding some of the public projects that are required in Canada. I deliberately set those dispatches in the context of Mr. Jodoin's appeal that there be a three-way conference to attack the problem of unemployment.
Halfway between Vancouver and Montreal, halfway between the Marpole bridge and the tunnels and the bridges they say they need in Montreal, is the important Canadian centre of Winnipeg, and we need a bridge there too. It is in connection with that bridge that I want to say a few words. As a matter of fact our traffic problems in the city of Winnipeg are so great that a number of bridges are sorely needed, but I ask the government to get ready to consider a particular request which I believe will be made to the federal government before long. That request will relate to what is known as the Disraeli bridge, which it is proposed should be built over the Red river in the constituency of Winnipeg North Centre to relieve the serious traffic congestion between downtown Winnipeg and the north end of the city.
The matter has been under consideration at the city level for some considerable time. Recently a delegation led by Mayor George Sharpe of the city of Winnipeg called on the provincial government asking it to provide aid toward the construction of the Disraeli bridge, and it has been suggested by the

Disraeli Bridge
city to the provincial government that it should approach the federal government to obtain its sanction of this project, a project of the kind that was envisaged in the famous green book proposals of 1945.
The amount of money involved in this bridge is peanuts compared with what they are asking in Montreal and is small compared with what is requested by Vancouver, but I draw the attention of the government as a whole and the Minister of Labour in particular, in view of my question to him earlier today, to the statement that has been made by the chief engineer of the city of Winnipeg, Mr. W. D. Hurst, that this project would provide work for 410 men for about two years. The total estimated cost of the Disraeli bridge project is of the order of $6 million, and it is expected that the labour cost would be of the order of $2,500,000.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I am speaking in general terms but also in specific terms. It does seem to me that the point made by President Jodoin of the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada is well put, that the time has come for a concerted attack on the serious problem of unemployment. He went on to say, in the dispatch from which I read a couple of paragraphs a few moments ago:
"It is no time for playing politics", he said. "It is time for all levels of government, employers and labour to get together to discuss this problem around the table and get some action."
I do not think it is necessary to press the point that, along with much needed action in housing and other fields, this whole field of public works projects is one in which something could be done for the good of the country in terms of relieving traffic congestion and improving our whole highway set-up, and in terms of improving the wealth of the country as a whole. It is also a field in which something very definite can be done to minimize unemployment.
I urge the Minister of Labour as strongly as I can to give serious consideration to the suggestion made by Mr. Jodoin. If I heard the minister correctly in the interchange we had this afternoon, I think he said he had not yet had a request directly from Mr. Jodoin himself. I hope he will not wait for a letter from the president of the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada, but rather that the very fact that such a conference has been suggested will prompt him to take action himself. It is not only a conference along the lines suggested for dealing with unemployment that I urge upon the government. I also urge the government as a whole to shake the dust off its green books of 1945 and make it clear to the country that they are now prepared to put federal money into public works

projects such as those that have been suggested by other members, and such as this bridge project that is sorely needed in the city of Winnipeg.
As I say, I expect that a formal request with respect to the Disraeli bridge project will come from the city of Winnipeg through the provincial government before very long. I hope that when it comes it will receive favourable consideration by the federal government, and that we can soon have the help we need on this very important project, both because we need the bridge and because we need employment in the city of Winnipeg.
Mr. Speaker, in taking part in this debate with respect to bridges-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I am informed that the hon. member who has just risen has already spoken on this motion. Is the motion carried?

Before we pass the motion to go into supply, Mr. Speaker, I have two related matters upon which I should like to say a word. They have to do with the unfair competition in the trucking industry, which is related also to the Pacific Great Eastern Railway in the province of British Columbia-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, I have not been in the house sufficiently long to have become familiar with the grievance practice that seems to have grown up in the past two years. My understanding is that my hon. friend cannot discuss anything which he could discuss when we get into supply. If he will begin by announcing the grievance he has in mind we might be able to judge whether or not it is in order.

Well, I am new in the house but my grievance is this. The subsidized railways are putting themselves in competition with the trucking industry to the point where it is ultimately going to destroy that industry.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: This has nothing whatever to do with the government moving into supply, and surely is not a grievance at this point that would hold up getting into committee of supply where we can discuss the expenditure of public money.

On the point of order, Mr. Speaker, I always understood that on the motion to go into supply one could raise any grievance. The minister could very well argue that any matters one wished to discuss could be discussed at some point on the estimates. How do we know whether or not

the minister is going to bring in the estimates of the Department of Transport immediately after this motion is passed? Surely it has always been the right of a member to raise any grievance, no matter what that grievance may be, on the motion to go into supply. I do not feel the minister is in order in saying that it should be a matter that could not be raised when we get on the estimates.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I think the hon. member must have misunderstood me, and I may have been at fault. I did not say anything about the estimates, but I did say something about getting into supply. I admit we have nothing in our estimates on the Pacific Great Eastern Railway, at least I do not think we have. But that is not the point. The point the hon. member was making was that subsidized railways, privately owned perhaps, are in competition with trucking. Now, is the point that this government should do something about that?

If I may speak to the point of order the minister has raised, Mr. Speaker, I would say that the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Leboe) came to me and asked whether I thought he would be in order in raising this matter, and I told him I thought he would. I thought so for this reason. The traditional picture is this. We go into supply for the purpose of asking the people of Canada to give some money to the crown. Traditionally, before we go into supply members who represent the people have a right to air a grievance before the crown gets any more money.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: A grievance against the crown?

Yes; that is the traditional pattern. The grievance the hon. member has is simply this, that this government collects money for the purpose of subsidizing railways. Now, before the house moves into committee of supply, the hon. member wants to say why we should not go into supply.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: You should not subsidize railways.
No, not necessarily, but he has a grievance in respect of that. It may be that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: You say you know what his grievance is; let us know.
Let him announce it.

My friends are not going to buffalo me like that. There have been a few other people airing grievances in this debate on the motion to go into supply which were no more justified than the one my hon. friend has.
Pacific Great Eastern Railway

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: That is your opinion.

That is my opinion, and my
opinion is just as substantial as that of the member for Halifax (Mr. Dickey).

It just happens he is at the
tail end, so he is getting impatient.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I do not want to do anything at all that would precipitate a longer debate than we have already had. If I understand my hon. friend intends to complain about the conduct of the government in some respects, this is the point at which to make the complaint and I withdraw anything I have said.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I am grateful to
hon. members who have just spoken to the point of order. I should like to refer to citation 467 in Beauchesne's third edition, which refers to a motion to go into committee of supply, and reads in part as follows:
When such motion is proposed, it shall be permissible to discuss any public matter within the powers of the federal parliament . . .
The opening remarks of the hon. member who took the floor did give me some concern because it seemed to me he intended to address himself to the regulation of truckers which, on the surface, would appear to be a provincial matter and would possibly not be the type of grievance which we would ordinarily hear at this time. I am merely drawing the hon. member's attention to this citation and asking him to co-operate in this respect, that any grievance which he raises should be a matter, in the words of the citation, "within the powers of the federal parliament".

Yes, Mr. Speaker; I shall
govern myself accordingly. What I want to deal with has to do with the federal government and the Department of Transport, I believe. The question resolves itself around something that is very important to the people in the northern interior of British Columbia. Their welfare, of course, is something about which I am greatly concerned.
The grievance is simply this, and I may state it again. The railways of Canada come under the Department of Transport, and by virtue of the fact that we vote moneys for these railways, particularly the Canadian National, they are able to transport goods for almost nothing. The Pacific Great Eastern Railway has a working agreement with a trucking concern that is known as a piggyback service from Vancouver into Dawson Creek, which is in competition with the subsidized Canadian National Railways. How we can expect any legitimate business to
1408	HOUSE OF
Pacific Great Eastern Railway carry on against a subsidized railway that can cut its rates to nothing is more than I can understand.
I asked whether or not there were going to be any grants to aid in the construction of this Pacific Great Eastern Railway. When I analysed the answer I got I saw in it the possibility of competition against the Pacific Great Eastern Railway, which would place that provincial railway in such a position that in the eyes of the federal government it would become uneconomical to operate.
Now, if the Pacific Great Eastern Railway cannot meet that competition and its business drops, naturally the railway will be in such a position that this government might as well come along and say, "We have no reason whatsoever for helping to build the railway any further into the northern part of the province, or for connecting Squamish with Vancouver". In that connection I should like to read from a report that appeared in the Prince George Citizen of February 3, 1955. It bears the heading "Major Railways hit P.G.E. with Low Freight Rate to Dawson Creek" and states:
The Pacific Great Eastern Railway stands to lose thousands of dollars in revenue unless it meets a new low Vancouver to Dawson Creek freight charge set by the C.N.R. and C.P.R., according to Frank Walden, special writer for the Vancouver Sun.
The P.G.E. hooked up 18 months ago at Prince George with a Dawson Creek trucking firm to offer lower freight rates to the north, and since then the national railways, operating on their old schedule, have lost considerable business.
Then the article goes on to explain the losses of the Pacific Great Eastern Railway and of the trucking industry. And, incidentally, anyone who is familiar with that part of the country knows that the trucking industry is very important to the welfare of that particular area. Later in the same article we find this:
The P.G.E. thus was able to quote a Vancouver to Dawson Creek freight rate for the first time. It was $3.50 a hundredweight for number one freight and $2.09 for number five.
Because of the shorter haul-700 miles less-* Vancouver wholesalers began selling immediately in Dawson Creek. Edmonton firms found their B.C. block business slipping.
The final cut on the rate, as I understand it, was another 74 cents below the figure I have just given. It appears to me that most certainly this is something that should be brought to the attention of the house with great force, and that we must get down to something in the nature of an arrangement under which the people of British Columbia will be protected. I believe the thinking of the people out there can be described best by


an editorial which appeared in the Dawson Creek Star of January 27, 1955, which states:
Collusion between the federal government and the two big railway companies to scuttle the Canadian truck freight service appears indicated in a recent announcement of a drastic reduction in freight rates. The announced 74 cents a hundred under the combined P.G.E. rail-truck rate from Vancouver to Dawson Creek is also seen as a crack at the previncially operated P.G.E. railway. Expansion plans of the latter railway to serve the fast growing Peace river country doesn't fit in with the stagnated thinking of Ottawa officials who in the past have been proven to be long on promises but short on action.
Fast and efficient service of reliable trucking companies has taken away from the railways much of the freight movement, particularly over shorter distances. Trucking companies have to improve and maintain good service to exist, not so the railways. Railways can always fall back on taxpayers subsidies when the going gets tough.
At a time when the railways are screaming for higher freight rates, the action of cutting to the bone the rate between Vancouver and Dawson Creek can only mean one thing-the elimination of truck hauling competition, then up will go the rail freight rate higher than ever.
And later in the same editorial:
Should the suggested cut in rail rates take place, as seems indicated, it means local trucking companies will suffer a setback which could put them out of business completely. Taxpayers will still be expected to subsidize the railways even when running at a considerable loss. And if railways don't admit they would be running at a loss under these conditions then there is no justification for asking for an increased tariff rate.
We suspect the main reason for the move is to get at the provincial government because of its announced plan to extend the P.G.E. railway into the Peace river country with its ultimate intention of pulling a portion of the freight traffic to the west. A somewhat "dog in the manger" attitude accounted for by the railways lack of ability to meet efficient operation of the truckers with equally efficient operation of their own business.
Just to review the situation briefly I should like to give some short quotations with a view to clarifying the position. I would quote first from page 1448 of Hansard, the second session of 1949. Mr. Chevrier, who was then minister of transport, said this:
The reasons for the construction of the Pacific Great Eastern were: (1) to provide an independent or direct route for the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway to the city of Vancouver, (2) to open the central portion of British Columbia; and (3) to provide an outlet for the Peace river country through Vancouver.
And to quote again from page 1450 of the same volume, we find the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair) speaking to a bill to bring assistance to the construction of the Pacific Great Eastern railway from Quesnel to Prince George. He said:
The P.G.E. of course will never be a profitable operation until the other gap is also completed, that is the gap between the village of Squamish and the city of Vancouver.

And again, at the same page:
I want to warn hon. members, however, that when this subsidy of $15,000 a mile for this construction is passed, I do not think it will be the last time this house will be asked to help in the extension of the P.G.E.
And again on the same page:
I want to just mention this briefly, because when we are passing this appropriation, I think we should be fully aware of all the implications, since we are committing ourselves to a policy of subsidizing the extension of this provincial railway.
I make these quotations only because they have a bearing on the problem. It will certainly be difficult for the Pacific Great Eastern Railway as well as for the provincial government if, because of unfair competition from subsidized federal railways, they have to show losses in their operations and receive lesser amounts for the freight they are carrying. I can see where this government could come back to the province of British Columbia and say, "You are not making any money. Why should we give any additional assistance toward the extension of that railway from Squamish, British Columbia, to Vancouver, or from Prince George into the great Peace river country?" That is why I bring this up at this time. It is very important to the people of that part of the country. We are looking forward to the day when the thinking of this government will be along the lines of the thinking in 1949 when grants were made to the provincial government to extend this railway.
I should like to see this matter cleared up in such a way that a reasonable charge can be made on freight going into the Peace river area so competition will be fair. If the railways were not being subsidized it would be a different situation, but since the railways are subsidized it puts the Pacific Great Eastern Railway and the truckers in an absolutely impossible situation. I hope the government will look into the matter and do something about it, because it certainly is worthy of attention.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Robinson (Simcoe East) in the chair.

Mr. Chairman, I must
apologize for rising to speak on the resolution at what appeared to be the wrong time, but I could not help recalling that the last time I rose to introduce a resolution on the War Veterans Allowance Act the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre insisted that I should make a statement before we went into committee, and we had quite a bit of argument over it.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE ALLOWANCES AND PERMISSIBLE INCOME, ETC.
speechtext:
However, as I was stating, the resolution now before the committee is consequent on the announcement made in the speech from the throne that the War Veterans Allowance Act, 1952, would be amended during the course of the present session. Hon. members will recall that this act was completely revised in 1952.
I realize that it would not be proper at this stage to give details of the legislation which will follow this resolution, but I am sure I will meet the wishes of hon. members by indicating what the salient points will be. The main effect of the amendments will be to increase the rate of the monthly allowance by 20 per cent. In other words, the allowance to qualified veterans and widows having the status of single persons will be increased from a maximum of $50 to $60, while that paid to veterans and widows who qualify for the married rate will be increased from $90 to $108.
At the same time it is proposed to increase the permissible income ceilings from $720 to $840 for recipients of the single rate and from $1,200 to $1,440 for recipients of the married rate. In the case of a married veteran whose spouse is blind within the meaning of the Blind Persons Act the income ceiling will be raised from the present rate of $1,320 to $1,560. There will be a proportionate increase in the ceilings applicable to orphans who qualify under the act for the allowance.
I believe these increases in rates and ceilings are in line with the general policy of making certain that the veterans charter is kept up to date and amended to meet changing conditions. I am sure the proposed amendments will be welcomed not only by those directly concerned but by Canadians generally, who do have a genuine and sympathetic interest in the welfare and well-being of our older veterans.
There is also a provision for extending the benefits of section 4 of the act to female veterans and to widows at the age of 55. As hon. members know, the payment of allowance under this section is made on a monthly rather than a yearly basis, which enables

the beneficiary to take employment for a limited period during the year without the entitlement to allowance during the remaining months of the year being affected by the earned income.
There will be certain other amendments, mostly of an administrative nature. As the resolution mentions, there will be provision for increasing the salaries of the members of the board.
In introducing this legislation I should like to express my appreciation to hon. members on both sides of the house, particularly those who have sat on the special committees on veterans affairs, who together with the various veterans organizations in Canada have been most helpful in presenting their studies and recommendations. As minister of the department charged with the responsibility of veterans affairs, I have no doubt that the amending legislation which will follow this resolution will raise appreciably the standard of living of many veterans and their dependents.

It does seem to me that the wishes of the Canadian Legion and members of the committees in past years could very well have been met.
The permissible income ceiling for single veterans has been raised from $720 to $840, an increase of $120. In my opinion this is not enough. However, we will hear more of this when the matter is discussed in the committee. The permissible income ceiling
War Veterans Allowance Act for married veterans has been increased from $1,200 to $1,440, an increase of $240. The members of the committee and the Canadian Legion asked that it be raised to $2,000. Again I say this increase is not going to satisfy many war veteran allowance recipients throughout this country.
I am glad to know that the provisions of section 4 are being extended to female veterans. While this may not seem to amount to very much it will be of great assistance to them.
As I said at the outset, it is not my intention to discuss this matter further. We will have that opportunity when the bill is before the committee. speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I believe that a fair reaction to the proposal announced this evening by the minister would be this. Why chisel; why not do the job right while we are at it? That, I think, sums up the weaknesses in the proposals made by the minister this evening. I need only go over the figures as they have been announced by him. Take for example, the case of a single veteran. He has been eligible for $50 a month plus permissive earnings of $10, making a total of $60. He is now to get a war veterans allowance of $60 a month, but he is still only eligible for permissive earnings in the same old amount of $10 a month.
Where does that leave him when he reaches the age of 70. Every other person in the country who reaches the age of 70 gets $40 a month automatically in addition to whatever he or she may be receiving on reaching that age. This has been one of the main complaints about the war veterans allowance, that when the veteran reached 70 years of age he did not get the full benefit of old age security. Under the ceiling announced by the minister this evening a veteran on reaching 70 years of age will still not be able to get the full amount of old age security. He will only get $10 a month, while the civilian who did not serve in the forces gets an increase in his actual cash receipts of $40 a month.
The war veterans allowance recipient will have been receiving $60 a month war veterans allowance, and then will only be allowed an additional $10 when he reaches the age of 70. I repeat this means that he can only get $10 by way of old age security payment instead of the full $40. The ceiling should have been made high enough so that a veteran on reaching 70 would get his war veterans allowance plus the full $40 old age security payment.
I point out to the minister that the unanimous recommendation of the special committee on veterans affairs of 1952 with respect to the war veterans allowance was in these words:
Your committee further recommends to the government continued and sympathetic study of the needs and requirements of recipients of war veterans allowance, keeping in mind the recommendations of veterans organizations in that respect and particularly with regard to permissive income.

War Veterans Allowance Act
That was the recommendation three years ago, and today we get this half measure after waiting for that period.
Last year the special committee on veterans affairs again made a recommendation which referred to the submissions made by the Canadian Legion, the national council of veterans associations and the Canadian non-pensioned veterans widows, particularly dealing with the changes they had urged in the War Veterans Allowance Act. The report refers to raising the amounts of allowances payable thereunder and also raising the level of permissive income. As hon. members know, some of us had tried to get better reports both in 1952 and last year, but this was the unanimous recommendation of the committee:
Your committee recommends that the government give sympathetic consideration to the said submissions.
I submit, Mr. Chairman, to you and to the members of the committee of this house that these changes are not good enough, particularly regarding the permissive income. This question will have to be fought out in the committee. I am confident that the veterans of this country are not going to be satisfied with such a small improvement with regard to permissive income. I repeat, why on earth should we chisel when at last we are in a position to do something about this War Veterans Allowance Act? Why not make the proper amendments when we have the opportunity to do so?
I am afraid, Mr. Chairman, that here again we have the government tying the war veterans allowance to the ordinary welfare legislation. This point was made by the minister himself last year when we were discussing war veterans allowances. He argued that we could not get too far away from the measures dealing with civilians. He took the same stand before the dominion convention of the Canadian Legion last summer. I have a newspaper report here of August 3 in which the minister is reported as having said at the dominion convention:
The allowances had always been linked with old age pensions and were specially designed to meet the needs of veterans with combat service.
"This being the case, any major changes in the War Veterans Allowance Act-as some which have been suggested-cannot help but have serious financial implications in other fields of government activities."
Well, the position is not the same at all. These men have a claim as of right for services rendered. These men were willing to risk their lives for this nation. The war veterans allowance recipient is a front-line soldier. The only other veteran who can qualify is one who is in receipt of a small pension, but primarily the war veterans allowance was for Canada's front-line fighting
men. They have a claim on this country as of right. Their claim is not in the same category at all as the claim of welfare recipients. I am not quarrelling for a minute with the payments made to others. I simply say that the basis of the claims is different. The two groups cannot be tied together. If they are, there never will be adequate justice done to the veterans of this nation.
Unfortunately these changes the minister has announced tonight seem to me to have been made on the basis of tying them in with all the other social welfare legislation. I can only express the hope that all of the members serving on the special committee on veterans affairs which is to be set up, as well as the general membership of the house, will not be satisfied with these provisions and will insist that the amendments be broadened out so they will do justice to the front-line veterans of the nation.

I, too, was very happy to hear the minister suggest that there was going to be a change in the War Veterans Allowance Act, for several reasons. However, Mr. Speaker, I agree completely with the hon. member who has just taken his seat.
There is one factor that should be taken into consideration that has not been thought of up to this time. It is that in British Columbia and Alberta the old age pensioner gets the regular $40 a month, and under a means test he gets an additional $15 which gives him $55 per month. This means $110 per month for a husband and wife. The married war veteran in this country today under the War Veterans Allowance Act is only permitted $108 per month. It is true the veteran is permitted to earn over and above that to a minor extent. I understood it was about $10 per month, and that is not a great deal.
I would find fault with the fact that there is no change in the amount of permissive income, as some of the members who spoke prior to me discovered. I do not rise to congratulate the minister at all, Mr. Chairman. Some members on this side of the house have suggested that he should be congratulated, but I do not think so. I feel this is a niggardly arrangement with regard to a problem of great importance in Canada.
Of course I have not been impressed with the activities of the minister of this department. I feel he has missed an opportunity on many occasions to do something effectively, powerfully and wholeheartedly in favour of the veterans. He has had an opportunity here on this question of war veterans allowances, and again he has missed that opportunity. He has come forward with a small concession. He introduced some camouflage talk about raising the ceiling on permissive income which on examination, as shown by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, is no change at all for single persons and for married veterans on war veterans allowance amounts to only $2 per month. It is just a bit of camouflage to make the thing appear better, and I think the minister should deal in a different way with matters of this nature.
Three years ago I pointed out, when we were discussing those receiving war veterans allowances, that their number is dwindling. The report of the department shows that they are dying off at the rate of a thousand a year. It is a declining obligation on the part of the government, so far as the veterans of the first world war are concerned; and that declining obligation would lead one to think that in circumstances such as these, with the rising cost of living and the increasing age of these men, some more generous arrangement might be made.
The government, however, is just trying to sit them out. They will all have died off before very long. The hon. member for Van-couver-Quadra pointed out the importance of the war veterans allowance-watered down by various ministerial interpretations in recent years-based, as it was originally, on service in an actual theatre of war. These men who are now 60 years of age and over are the ones who served in a theatre of war but were not wounded. They went through the same experiences as anyone else who was over there but, fortunately, they were not


wounded. The fact remains that they certainly suffered as much as any of the disability pensioners from their experiences in the trenches and from the general activities of the campaign between 1914 and 1918.
Unfortunately people are beginning to forget what occurred during that war. I propose that the Minister of National Defence should get busy and have completed the official history of that war so that people who are discussing this problem affecting our citizens on war veterans allowances will know something about what those men went through during that period of time. I took this matter up with his predecessor. However, the story has not been told officially, and we are beginning to forget it. Certain people are glossing it over, and are trying to pretend that these men are in the same category as civilians who are receiving assistance under the old age security program.
I hope the committee will deal at greater length with the points mentioned in the bill.

Aircraft Warning Systems

subtopic: JOINT ANNOUNCEMENT RESPECTING AIRCRAFT WARNING SYSTEMS, SEPTEMBER 27, 1954

speechtext:
On April 8, 1954, the governments of Canada and the United States issued a joint announcement, which after referring to the construction of the "Pinetree" radar chain, announced plans for the establishment of a further radar system "generally to the north of the settled territory in Canada". The Canadian government subsequently decided that it would be appropriate, as a part of its contribution to the common defence requirements of the two countries, for Canada to undertake responsibility for financing, constructing and operating this new system, which is generally referred to as the "mid-Canada line".
During the time that plans for the mid-Canada line have been under development, studies have also been going on to determine the feasibility of providing even earlier warning of the approach of hostile aircraft. As a result of these studies, the Canadian and United States governments have agreed in principle that there is a need for the establishment of a distant early warning line across the far northern part of North America, and have directed that detailed planning for such a line should be initiated at once. The basis of participation by the two countries in the construction and operation of the line, and the division of costs, will be determined after the detailed plans have been considered and agreed.
In developing the complete system for warning of the approach of hostile aircraft and for the control of interceptor forces, the two governments have followed a policy building outward from the likely target areas. Thus the first step, which has now been largely completed, was the construction of the main control and warning radar installations in the continental United States and the populated part of Canada. The second step, which is now under way, is the provision of the mid-Canada line. A third measure, the need for which has now been agreed upon between the two governments, will be the provision of a distant early warning line across the most northerly practicable part of North America. Portions of the complete warning and control system in Canada will be extended to seaward on both flanks of the continent by the United States.
The establishment of these North American defence installations is a costly and difficult task, which is being undertaken because our security requires it and is being accomplished successfully because of the readiness of Canadians and Americans to work together in a common cause.

subtopic: JOINT ANNOUNCEMENT RESPECTING AIRCRAFT WARNING SYSTEMS, NOVEMBER 19, 1954

speechtext:
On September 27, 1954, the defence departments of Canada and the United States issued a joint announcement on the progress being made in the development of a comprehensive jointly operated system for warning of the approach of hostile aircraft and for the control of interceptor aircraft. Four main elements of a warning and control system now appear to be practicable, namely: the main control and warning radar installations in the populated part of Canada (the jointly operated "Pinetree" network) and in the United States, which are now in operation; a warning line north of the settled areas of Canada (the mid-Canada line) being built by Canada; a warning line across the most northerly practicable part of North America (the distant early warning line); and portions of the complete warning and control system in Canada to be extended to seaward on both flanks of the continent by the United States.
In the announcement of September 27, it was stated that the Canadian and United States governments had agreed in principle
that there was a need for a distant early warning line across the far northern part of North America and had directed that detailed planning for such a line should be initiated at once.
As a consequence of the progress which has been made since the announcement last September, the two governments have now decided to proceed with the construction of the distant early warning line.
Experience has shown that projects of this nature can be carried out most effectively by vesting responsibility for all phases of the work of construction and installation in a single authority. In the joint statement of September 27, referred to above, it was announced that Canada had undertaken the responsibility for the construction of the mid-Canada line. In the case of the distant early warning line it has been agreed that although both Canada and the United States will participate in the project, responsibility for the work of construction and installation should be vested in the United States.
